Civil laws: State unfair and deceptive practices laws (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17200, 17500; Fla. Stat. § 501.204; Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46)
Preventive rules: FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45)

If the AI were a legal person: Section 230 question, same either way (company recommended others' content)
Barriers to liability: Section 230, First Amendment, Damages or standing
Human precedent for each law: RF-FTC5: United States v. Epic Games, Inc., No. 5:22-cv-00518 (E.D.N.C. Feb. 7, 2023) (stipulated order for permanent injunction and civil penalty judgment) [Consent order]; VS-UDAP: People of the State of California v. Meta Platforms, Inc., 753 F. Supp. 3d 849 (N.D. Title: New York City Reportedly Released Disputed Value-Added Teacher Ratings for Thousands of Teachers
Description: After a legal dispute over public-records requests, the New York City Department of Education released Teacher Data Reports that used a value-added statistical model to rate thousands of public-school teachers based on estimated student test-score growth. News outlets published the ratings in February 2012, and teachers, unions, and analysts disputed the scores as imprecise and potentially misleading, citing large error margins, limited samples, and apparent roster-linkage errors.
Harmed parties: teachers, students, new-york-city-teachers, new-york-city-students, epistemic-integrity, educational-communities
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A school district official who rated teachers with an imprecise statistical formula and released the error-prone ratings under a public-records order.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Release was compelled by public-records litigation, and imprecise evaluations of public employees are not actionable absent a tangible employment action shown here.
Reasoning note: Ratings are statistical opinions released under legal compulsion; press publication is protected. No firing or discipline based on scores appears in the record.

Civil laws: Section 1983 (constitutional torts by state actors) (42 U.S.C. § 1983); False arrest, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution (Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 35, 653); State anti-discrimination statutes (Cal. Gov. Code § 12940 (FEHA); Cal. Civ. Code § 51 (Unruh Act); N.Y. Exec. Law § 296); California Government Claims Act (Cal. Gov't Code §§ 815, 815.2, 820.2, 945.4)
Preventive rules: Maryland limits on police facial recognition (Md. Code Ann., Crim. Proc. §§ 2-501, 2-503); San Francisco ban on city use of face recognition (S.F. Admin. Code § 19B.2(d)); New York City POST Act (police surveillance technology) (N.Y.C. Admin. Code § 14-188 (Local Law 65 of 2020))
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty; As maker of a defective product
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Human precedent for each law: VF-1983: Gatlin v. Welle, No. 4:25-cv-00043 (E.D. Mo. Oct. 15, 2025) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-GOV-TORT: Bell v. State of California, 63 Cal. App. 4th 919, 74 Cal. Rptr. 2d 541 (1998) [Claim allowed to proceed]; RL-NYC-POST: OIG-NYPD, An Assessment of NYPD's Response to the POST Act (facial recognition technology findings), N.Y.C. Dep't of Investigation, Office of the Inspector General for the NYPD, An Assessment of NYPD's Response to the POST Act (Nov. 2022) [Regulatory action]; VS-FALSE-IMPRISON: Perryman v. City of Bloomington, 704 F. Supp. 3d 961 (D. Minn. 2023) [Claim allowed to proceed]; CF-COLOR-LAW: United States v. McDermott, 918 F.2d 319 (2d Cir. 1990) [Conviction]; VS-STATE-CIVIL-RIGHTS: Candelore v. Tinder, Inc., 19 Cal. App. 5th 1138 (2018) [Claim allowed to proceed]; RL-SF-FRT-BAN: SFPD Disciplinary Review Board, Second Quarter 2022 Findings and Recommendations (policy failure finding: officer's improper use of facial recognition technology), Letter from William Scott, Chief of Police, to the San Francisco Police Commission, Re: Second Quarter 2022 Disciplinary Review Board Findings and Recommendations (Oct. 7, 2022) [Regulatory action]
Reasoning note: Color-of-law crime needs willfulness, not shown. Arrest resting on an unreliable match states Fourth Amendment and false arrest claims; qualified immunity is the main obstacle.

Title: Google Instant's Allegedly 'Anti-Semitic' Results Lead To Lawsuit In France
Description: The organizations SOS Racisme, Union of Jewish Students of France, Movement Against Racism and for Friendship Among Peoples are suing Google due to its autocomplete software suggesting "jewish" when the names of certain public figures were searched on the platform.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A reference librarian who, when patrons typed certain public figures' names, suggested the word Jewish next to them.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Associating a person with a religion is not defamatory or unlawful in the US; French limits on ethnic and religious data have no US analog.
Real-world action reported: Antiracism groups sued Google in France
Reasoning note: Suggestions reflect other users' queries.

Title: Buenos Aires Government Reportedly Used Children's Personal Data in Facial Recognition System for Fugitives
Description: Beginning in April 2019, the Buenos Aires city government reportedly used data from Argentina’s CONARC fugitive database, including children’s identities and reference photos, in its live Facial Recognition System for Fugitives (SRFP). Human Rights Watch found at least 166 children had appeared in CONARC between 2017 and 2020 and warned that the system exposed them to privacy violations and elevated risks of false matches.
Harmed parties: privacy, minors, general-public-of-buenos-aires, general-public-of-argentina, general-public, buenos-aires-children, biometric-data-subjects
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A city police unit that loaded children's names and photos from a fugitive list into street cameras to scan crowds for them.
Civil laws: Section 1983 (constitutional torts by state actors) (42 U.S.C. § 1983); Invasion of privacy torts (Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 652B-652E); California Government Claims Act (Cal. Gov't Code §§ 815, 815.2, 820.2, 945.4)
Preventive rules: Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code ch. 552 (Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, H.B. 149 (2025)), e.g., § 552.052); Maryland limits on police facial recognition (Md. Code Ann., Crim. Proc. §§ 2-501, 2-503); San Francisco ban on city use of face recognition (S.F. Admin. Code § 19B.2(d)); New York City POST Act (police surveillance technology) (N.Y.C. Admin. Code § 14-188 (Local Law 65 of 2020))
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Human precedent for each law: VF-1983: Hassan v. City of New York, 804 F.3d 277 (3d Cir. 2015), as amended (Feb. 2, 2016) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-GOV-TORT: Doe v. County of San Diego, 445 F. Supp. 3d 957 (S.D. Cal. 2020) [Claim allowed to proceed]; RL-NYC-POST: OIG-NYPD, An Assessment of NYPD's Response to the POST Act (facial recognition technology findings), N.Y.C. Dep't of Investigation, Office of the Inspector General for the NYPD, An Assessment of NYPD's Response to the POST Act (Nov. 2022) [Regulatory action]; RL-SF-FRT-BAN: SFPD Disciplinary Review Board, Second Quarter 2022 Findings and Recommendations (policy failure finding: officer's improper use of facial recognition technology), Letter from William Scott, Chief of Police, to the San Francisco Police Commission, Re: Second Quarter 2022 Disciplinary Review Board Findings and Recommendations (Oct. 7, 2022) [Regulatory action]
Reasoning note: Juvenile record confidentiality laws, the closest US fit, are not in the library. No specific false stop is reported; Fourth Amendment limits on public face scanning are unsettled.

Title: Knightscope's Park Patrol Robot Ignored Bystander Pressing Emergency Button to Alert Police about Fight
Description: A Knightscope K5 autonomous "police" robot patrolling Huntington Park, California failed to respond to an onlooker who attempted to activate its emergency alert button when a nearby fight broke out.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A park security guard who ignored a bystander's pleas to call police while a fight broke out nearby.
Civil laws: Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7)
How the company is reached: As principal or employer (agency); As maker of a defective product
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Human precedent for each law: VS-NEGLIGENCE: Indian Towing Co. v. United States, 350 U.S. 61 (1955) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: No general duty to rescue; a claim needs an assumed duty via the emergency button plus reliance, and the fighters' acts are an intervening cause.

Title: International Baccalaureate’s 2020 Calculated-Grades Model Reportedly Lowered Students' Scores and College Prospects
Description: After Covid-19 canceled May 2020 exams, the Geneva-based International Baccalaureate reportedly used a calculated-grades model based on coursework, predicted grades, and historical school results to estimate final marks. Students, parents, and teachers reportedly said the opaque model produced unexpectedly low scores, threatening university admissions, scholarships, and study plans across multiple countries.
Harmed parties: international-baccalaureate-students, students, minors, teachers, parents, educational-communities, university-applicants
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: An exam board that set final grades with a formula weighted by schools' past results, lowering many students' marks.
Civil laws: Breach of contract and warranty (U.C.C. §§ 2-313, 2-314 (e.g., Cal. Com. Code §§ 2313, 2314))
Preventive rules: Colorado automated decision-making technology law (SB 26-189, replacing the 2024 Colorado AI Act) (Colo. S.B. 26-189 (2026), repealing and reenacting S.B. 24-205)
How the company is reached: As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Barriers to liability: Outside US reach, Damages or standing
Human precedent for each law: VS-WARRANTY-CONTRACT: Dalton v. Educational Testing Service, 87 N.Y.2d 384 (1995) [Liability found]
Reasoning note: Students paid for assessment; a contract claim needs terms promising individual assessment. No protected-class disparity is reported.

Title: Kidney Testing Method Allegedly Underestimated Risk of Black Patients
Description: Decades-long use of the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) method to test kidney function which considers race has been criticized by physicians and medical students for its racist history and inaccuracy against Black patients.
Who did the harm: How the system was built, trained, or marketed
If a human did it: A medical guideline committee that told doctors to adjust kidney test results upward for Black patients, delaying their diagnosis and care.
Civil laws: ACA section 1557 (discrimination in health programs) (42 U.S.C. § 18116(a)); State anti-discrimination statutes (Cal. Gov. Code § 12940 (FEHA); Cal. Civ. Code § 51 (Unruh Act); N.Y. Exec. Law § 296)
Preventive rules: Colorado automated decision-making technology law (SB 26-189, replacing the 2024 Colorado AI Act) (Colo. S.B. 26-189 (2026), repealing and reenacting S.B. 24-205); Section 1557 rule on patient care decision support tools (45 C.F.R. § 92.210 (89 Fed. Reg. 37692 (May 6, 2024)))
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Human precedent for each law: VS-STATE-CIVIL-RIGHTS: Louis v. SafeRent Solutions, LLC, 685 F. Supp. 3d 19 (D. Mass. 2023) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: An express race coefficient is a racial classification in a clinical tool; ACA section 1557 reaches federally funded health programs and its 2024 rule covers decision-support tools. Per-patient harm is unproven.

Title: AI mistakes referee’s bald head for football — hilarity ensued
Description: In a Scottish soccer match the AI-enabled ball-tracking camera used to livestream the game repeatedly tracked an official’s bald head as though it were the soccer ball.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
If a human did it: A camera operator who kept filming a linesman's bald head instead of the ball.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: A poor livestream annoyed viewers but is not a legal wrong.
Reasoning note: Viewer inconvenience only.

Title: Researchers find evidence of racial, gender, and socioeconomic bias in chest X-ray classifiers
Description: A study by the University of Toronto, the Vector Institute, and MIT showed the input databases that trained AI systems used to classify chest X-rays led the systems to show gender, socioeconomic, and racial biases.
Harmed parties: economically-vulnerable-patients, hispanic-patients, women-and-girls, patients, medicaid-beneficiaries, women
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
If a human did it: A radiologist who, in a study rather than patient care, missed disease more often in women, Hispanic, and Medicaid patients.
Preventive rules: FDA medical device premarket review (incl. software as a medical device) (21 U.S.C. §§ 360(k), 360c, 360e); Section 1557 rule on patient care decision support tools (45 C.F.R. § 92.210 (89 Fed. Reg. 37692 (May 6, 2024)))
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Reasoning note: Research finding; no patient harmed in care is identified. Imaging software is a device whose premarket review should test subgroup performance; covered providers must also mitigate discrimination risk from such tools.

Title: #LekkiMassacre: Why Facebook labelled content from October 20 incident ‘false’
Description: Facebook incorrectly labels content relating to an incident between #EndSARS protestors and the Nigerian army as misinformation.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A newspaper fact-checker who wrongly stamped accurate reports of soldiers firing on protesters as false.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Platform fact-check labels are protected editorial judgments; courts treat them as opinion (Stossel v. Meta), so mislabeled posters have no claim.
Reasoning note: Harm was suppression of accurate news, which no US law remedies against a private platform.

Title: AI Spam Filters Allegedly Block Legitimate Emails Based on Biased Keyword Detection
Description: AlgorithmWatch tested spam filtering algorithms across Gmail, Yahoo, Outlook, GMX, and LaPoste. Their findings reportedly showed that Microsoft Outlook’s spam filter flagged emails based on specific keywords that led to racial and content-based biases blocking legitimate communications. Emails mentioning Nigeria or containing certain financial and sexual health terms were found to be disproportionately marked as spam.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
If a human did it: A mailroom clerk who, in a test, set aside letters mentioning Nigeria or sexual health as junk.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Spam filtering is protected under s230(c)(2), and no law requires private email providers to deliver every message.
Reasoning note: Tester findings; no identified user lost a legal right.

Title: Tiny Changes Let False Claims About COVID-19, Voting Evade Facebook Fact Checks
Description: Avaaz, an international advocacy group, released a review of Facebook's misinformation identifying software showing that the labeling process failed to label 42% of false information posts, most surrounding COVID-19 and the 2020 USA Presidential Election.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A fact-check desk that missed 42 percent of false posts about COVID-19 and the election.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: No US law requires a platform to label or remove false posts; under-enforcement of its own policy is not actionable.
Reasoning note: Third-party misinformation is shielded by s230.

Title: AI attempts to ease fear of robots, blurts out it can’t ‘avoid destroying humankind’
Description: On September 8, 2020, the Guardian published an op-ed generated by OpenAI’s GPT-3 text generating AI that included threats to destroy humankind. This incident has been downgraded to an issue as it does not meet current ingestion criteria.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
If a human did it: A columnist who wrote an op-ed saying he could not avoid destroying humankind, with no one threatened.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Hyperbolic statements with no targeted person are not true threats; protected speech.
Reasoning note: Edited op-ed published by a newspaper; downgraded to an issue.

Title: Ireland's 2020 Leaving Certificate Calculated-Grades Model Reportedly Issued Incorrect Scores to Thousands of Students
Description: After Covid-19 disrupted the 2020 Leaving Certificate exams, Ireland's Department of Education and Skills used a calculated-grades model to issue student results on September 7. The Department later confirmed coding errors in how the model handled Junior Cycle data, resulting in incorrect grades. About 6,100 students received upgraded results, and college-offer eligibility had to be reassessed.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: An exam office clerk whose calculation mistakes gave about 6,100 students lower grades than they earned, upending college offers.
Preventive rules: Colorado automated decision-making technology law (SB 26-189, replacing the 2024 Colorado AI Act) (Colo. S.B. 26-189 (2026), repealing and reenacting S.B. 24-205)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Gap note: US courts reject educational-malpractice negligence claims, grading errors rarely implicate a protected property interest, and the grades were corrected.
Reasoning note: Errors were acknowledged and upgraded; harm was delay and lost offers, reassessed by colleges.

Title: UK passport photo checker shows bias against dark-skinned women
Description: UK passport photo checker shows bias against dark-skinned women.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A passport office clerk who more often rejected photos of dark-skinned women as poor quality.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: A photo-check tool applicants could override is not reachable without intent; Title VI does not bind federal agencies and equal protection needs intent.
Reasoning note: Disparate performance is documented, but no denied passport is reported.

Title: "Jewish Baby Strollers" Provided Anti-Semitic Google Images, Allegedly Resulting from Hate Speech Campaign
Description: Google's Image search for "Jewish baby strollers" showed offensive, anti-Semitic results, allegedly a result of a coordinated hate-speech campaign involving malicious actors on 4chan.
Who did the harm: A person used AI as the tool
Secondary structure: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A group of trolls who flooded a public photo catalog with anti-Semitic images labeled as baby strollers.
How the company is reached: Only as supplier of a misused tool
If the AI were a legal person: Same either way: company only supplied a tool a person misused
Gap note: Anti-Semitic images with no targeted person or threat are protected hate speech, and the search engine is shielded for third-party content.
Reasoning note: Coordinated manipulation of rankings by 4chan users; offensive but lawful.

Title: The Christchurch shooter and YouTube’s radicalization trap
Description: A New Zealand government report released following a right-wing terrorist killing 51 worshippers at two New Zealand mosques which indicated that Youtube's recommendation algorithm played an important role in the terrorist's radicalization.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A bookseller who kept recommending ever more extreme far-right material to a customer who later murdered 51 worshippers.
Civil laws: Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7); Product liability: design defect and failure to warn (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability §§ 1, 2; Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., 785 F. Supp. 3d 1157 (M.D. Fla. 2025)); Wrongful death and survival actions (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 377.60; Fla. Stat. §§ 768.16-.26)
How the company is reached: As maker of a defective product
If the AI were a legal person: Section 230 question, same either way (company recommended others' content)
Barriers to liability: Section 230, First Amendment, Causation, Outside US reach
Gap note: Hooks are weak: Twitter v. Taamneh found recommendations are not knowing assistance, and the shooter's crimes are a superseding cause.
Reasoning note: Recommending lawful extremist speech is not a crime without knowledge of the plan. The Anti-Terrorism Act remedy (VF-ATA) does not fit: no designated terrorist organization, and Taamneh requires knowing substantial assistance.

Title: Frontline workers protest at Stanford after hospital distributed vaccine to administrators
Description: In 2020, Stanford Medical Center's distribution algorithm only designated 7 of 5,000 vaccines to Medical Residents, who are frontline workers regularly exposed to COVID-19.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A hospital administrator whose vaccine priority list gave only 7 of 5,000 doses to frontline residents.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Prioritizing older staff violates no law: the ADEA protects only workers 40 and over, and the Age Discrimination Act, which covers all ages in funded programs, excludes employment practices.
Reasoning note: Policy choice harmful to residents but not a legal wrong.

Title: Apple Card's Credit Assessment Algorithm Allegedly Discriminated against Women
Description: Apple Card's credit assessment algorithm was reported by Goldman-Sachs customers to have shown gender bias, in which men received significantly higher credit limits than women with equal credit qualifications.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A credit officer who gave men much higher credit limits than women with equal credit qualifications.
Civil laws: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (15 U.S.C. § 1691); State anti-discrimination statutes (Cal. Gov. Code § 12940 (FEHA); Cal. Civ. Code § 51 (Unruh Act); N.Y. Exec. Law § 296)
Preventive rules: Regulation B adverse action notices (12 C.F.R. § 1002.9); Colorado automated decision-making technology law (SB 26-189, replacing the 2024 Colorado AI Act) (Colo. S.B. 26-189 (2026), repealing and reenacting S.B. 24-205)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty; As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Human precedent for each law: VS-STATE-CIVIL-RIGHTS: Louis v. SafeRent Solutions, LLC, 685 F. Supp. 3d 19 (D. Mass. 2023) [Claim allowed to proceed]; RF-REGB: Carroll v. Exxon Co., USA, 434 F. Supp. 557 (E.D. La. 1977) [Liability found]; VF-ECOA: Oliver v. Navy Federal Credit Union, No. 1:23-cv-01731 (E.D. Va. May 30, 2024), aff'd in part, vacated in part on other grounds, 167 F.4th 106 (4th Cir. 2026) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: A reported sex-based disparity at equal qualifications states an ECOA claim; whether qualifications were truly equal is the factual dispute. Goldman as creditor owes ECOA duties regardless of tool.

Title: HUD charges Facebook with enabling housing discrimination
Description: In March 2019 the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development charged Facebook with violating the Fair Housing Act by allowing real estate sellers to target advertisements in a discriminatory manner.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
Secondary structure: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: An advertising agency that let housing advertisers keep their ads from people by national origin, religion, and disability-related interests.
Civil laws: Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. §§ 3604, 3605)
Preventive rules: Colorado automated decision-making technology law (SB 26-189, replacing the 2024 Colorado AI Act) (Colo. S.B. 26-189 (2026), repealing and reenacting S.B. 24-205)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Real-world action reported: HUD charged Facebook under the Fair Housing Act (2019)
Human precedent for each law: VF-FHA: United States v. Meta Platforms, Inc., f/k/a Facebook, Inc., No. 22 Civ. 5187 (S.D.N.Y. June 27, 2022) (settlement agreement and final judgment) [Consent order]
Court or agency case about this incident: Secretary of HUD v. Facebook, Inc. (HUD Charge of Discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. 3604(a),(b),(c),(f)); after Facebook's election, resolved in United States v. Meta Platforms, Inc., HUD FHEO No. 01-18-0323-8 (charge issued 2019-03-28); United States v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 1:22-cv-05187 (S.D.N.Y.)
Reasoning note: FHA bars discriminatory housing advertising by any publisher; Facebook designed the targeting categories, so it is a content developer under Roommates and s230 is weak.

Title: Court Rules Deliveroo Used 'Discriminatory' Algorithm
Description: In December 2020, an Italian court ruled that Deliveroo’s employee ‘reliability’ algorithm illegally discriminated against workers with legitimate reasons for cancelling shifts.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A dispatch manager who downgraded couriers for any missed shift, even when they missed it for illness, emergencies, or a strike.
Civil laws: ADA Title I (employment) (42 U.S.C. § 12112); State anti-discrimination statutes (Cal. Gov. Code § 12940 (FEHA); Cal. Civ. Code § 51 (Unruh Act); N.Y. Exec. Law § 296); Family and Medical Leave Act interference and retaliation (29 U.S.C. §§ 2615(a), 2617(a))
Preventive rules: Colorado automated decision-making technology law (SB 26-189, replacing the 2024 Colorado AI Act) (Colo. S.B. 26-189 (2026), repealing and reenacting S.B. 24-205); Illinois Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act; IHRA AI amendment (820 ILCS 42; 775 ILCS 5/2-102(L)); National Labor Relations Act unfair labor practices (29 U.S.C. §§ 157, 158(a)(1), (a)(3))
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Barriers to liability: Outside US reach, No duty owed
Real-world action reported: Italian court ruled the algorithm discriminatory (Dec 2020)
Human precedent for each law: VS-STATE-CIVIL-RIGHTS: Mobley v. Workday, Inc., No. 3:23-cv-00770-RFL, ECF No. 360 (N.D. Cal. June 22, 2026) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VF-ADA1: Humphrey v. Memorial Hospitals Ass'n, 239 F.3d 1128 (9th Cir. 2001) [Liability found]; VF-FMLA: Bachelder v. America West Airlines, Inc., 259 F.3d 1112 (9th Cir. 2001) [Liability found]; RF-NLRA: NLRB v. Great Dane Trailers, Inc., 388 U.S. 26 (1967) [Liability found]
Reasoning note: US fit depends on employee status: penalizing strike absences implicates the NLRA, and illness absences FMLA leave or the ADA where disability-related.

Title: Job Screening Service Halts Facial Analysis of Applicants
Description: In January 2021, HireVue removed the controversial AI expression tracking tool from its virtual job interview software.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
Secondary structure: How the system was built, trained, or marketed
If a human did it: A hiring screener who scored job candidates on their facial expressions during video interviews.
Civil laws: ADA Title I (employment) (42 U.S.C. § 12112); Title VII (employment discrimination, incl. disparate impact) (42 U.S.C. §§ 2000e-2(a), 2000e-2(k)); Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (740 ILCS 14/15, 14/20); Texas and Washington biometric identifier laws (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 503.001; Wash. Rev. Code § 19.375.020)
Preventive rules: Illinois Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act; IHRA AI amendment (820 ILCS 42; 775 ILCS 5/2-102(L)); New York City automated employment decision tool law (Local Law 144) (N.Y.C. Admin. Code §§ 20-870 to 20-874); Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures (29 C.F.R. pt. 1607); Colorado automated decision-making technology law (SB 26-189, replacing the 2024 Colorado AI Act) (Colo. S.B. 26-189 (2026), repealing and reenacting S.B. 24-205); FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty; As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Human precedent for each law: RF-FTC5: Federal Trade Commission v. Rite Aid Corporation, No. 2:23-cv-05023 (E.D. Pa.), Stipulated Order for Permanent Injunction, ECF No. 19 (signed Feb. 23, 2024; entered Feb. 26, 2024) [Consent order]; VS-BIPA: Deyerler v. HireVue, Inc., No. 1:22-cv-01284 (N.D. Ill. Feb. 26, 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-BIOMETRIC-STATE: State of Texas v. Google LLC (Texas Attorney General CUBI action, Midland County), Civil enforcement action in Midland County under Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 503.001 and the DTPA (cause number not shown in the sources read), described in In re Google, LLC, 705 S.W.3d 479 (Tex. App. 2025) (No. 15-24-00090-CV, orig. proceeding); later resolved in the AG's $1.375 billion settlement with Google [Consent order]; VF-TITLE7: Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 401 U.S. 424 (1971) [Liability found]; RF-UGESP: Bradley v. City of Lynn, 443 F. Supp. 2d 145 (D. Mass. 2006) [Liability found]; VF-ADA1: Mobley v. Workday, Inc., 740 F. Supp. 3d 796 (N.D. Cal. 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: Expression scoring can screen out disabled applicants and needs validation; biometric laws reach face geometry of Illinois, Texas, and Washington applicants. Record shows the tool was dropped, not specific rejected applicants.

Title: Houston ISD's EVAAS Teacher-Evaluation System Reportedly Put Teachers' Jobs at Risk Through Unverifiable Scores
Description: From 2011 to 2015, Houston Independent School District used SAS Institute’s Education Value-Added Assessment System (EVAAS) to rate teacher effectiveness from student test-score growth. Teachers alleged that proprietary, unverifiable EVAAS scores contributed to terminations and contract nonrenewals. On May 4, 2017, a federal judge allowed due-process claims over the system to proceed.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A school district evaluator who fired or declined to renew teachers based on secret scores the teachers could not check.
Civil laws: Section 1983 (constitutional torts by state actors) (42 U.S.C. § 1983)
Preventive rules: Colorado automated decision-making technology law (SB 26-189, replacing the 2024 Colorado AI Act) (Colo. S.B. 26-189 (2026), repealing and reenacting S.B. 24-205)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Real-world action reported: Federal judge let teachers' due process claims proceed (2017)
Human precedent for each law: VF-1983: Houston Federation of Teachers, Local 2415 v. Houston Independent School District, 251 F. Supp. 3d 1168 (S.D. Tex. 2017) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Court or agency case about this incident: Houston Federation of Teachers, Local 2415 v. Houston Independent School District, 251 F. Supp. 3d 1168 (S.D. Tex. 2017); No. 4:14-cv-01189 (S.D. Tex.)
Reasoning note: Using unverifiable scores to take away a protected job interest denies a meaningful chance to contest the basis, a procedural due process claim against the district.

Title: Tesla Autopilot Mistakes Red Letters on Flag for Red Traffic Lights
Description: A Tesla Model 3 misidentified flags with "COOP" written vertically on them as traffic lights.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
If a human did it: A driver who mistook red lettering on flags for red traffic lights, with no crash.
How the company is reached: No path

If a human did it: A babysitter who, when a ten-year-old asked for a challenge, told her to touch a penny to the prongs of a half-plugged-in charger.
Crime if a human did it: Yes, if the required mental state is shown
Criminal laws: Child endangerment (Cal. Penal Code § 273a); Reckless endangerment (N.Y. Penal Law §§ 120.20, 120.25)
Civil laws: Product liability: design defect and failure to warn (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability §§ 1, 2; Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., 785 F. Supp. 3d 1157 (M.D. Fla. 2025)); Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7)
How the company is reached: As maker of a defective product; As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Section 230 question, same either way (company recommended others' content)
Human precedent for each law: VS-NEGLIGENCE: Anderson v. TikTok, Inc., 116 F.4th 180 (3d Cir. 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-PRODUCTS: Anderson v. TikTok, Inc., 116 F.4th 180 (3d Cir. 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; CS-ENDANGER: Minor v. State, 326 Md. 436, 605 A.2d 138 (1992) [Conviction]; CS-CHILD-ENDANGER: People v. Valdez, 27 Cal. 4th 778, 42 P.3d 511 (2002) [Conviction]
Reasoning note: Child endangerment needs willfulness or criminal negligence about the shock risk; the child was not hurt, so damages are thin. The suggestion was Alexa's own output, answering a 230 defense.

Title: Facebook's Ad Delivery Reportedly Excluded Audience along Racial and Gender Lines
Description: Facebook's housing and employment ad delivery process allegedly resulted in skews in exposure for some users along demographic lines such as gender and racial identity.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: An advertising agent who chose to show housing and job ads mostly to men or mostly to white people even when advertisers targeted everyone.
Civil laws: Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. §§ 3604, 3605); Title VII (employment discrimination, incl. disparate impact) (42 U.S.C. §§ 2000e-2(a), 2000e-2(k)); State anti-discrimination statutes (Cal. Gov. Code § 12940 (FEHA); Cal. Civ. Code § 51 (Unruh Act); N.Y. Exec. Law § 296); California Unruh Civil Rights Act and Disabled Persons Act (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 51(b), (f), 52(a), 54.1, 54.3; Munson v. Del Taco, Inc., 46 Cal. 4th 661, 670 (2009))
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Human precedent for each law: VS-STATE-CIVIL-RIGHTS: Liapes v. Facebook, Inc., 95 Cal. App. 5th 910 (2023) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VF-TITLE7: People of the State of Illinois v. Xing Ying Employment Agency, No. 1:15-cv-10235 (N.D. Ill. Mar. 20, 2018) [Liability found]; VS-UNRUH-DPA: Liapes v. Facebook, Inc., 95 Cal. App. 5th 910 (2023) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VF-FHA: United States v. Meta Platforms, Inc., f/k/a Facebook, Inc., No. 22 Civ. 5187 (S.D.N.Y. June 27, 2022) (settlement agreement and final judgment) [Consent order]
Reasoning note: The FHA bars discriminatory housing advertising, including skewed delivery; Title VII reach depends on the platform acting as an employment agency. California's Unruh Act reaches the platform's own delivery choices among its users.

Title: ETS Used Allegedly Flawed Voice Recognition Evidence to Accuse and Assess Scale of Cheating, Causing Thousands to be Deported from the UK
Description: International testing organization ETS admits voice recognition as evidence of cheating for thousands of previous TOEIC test-takers that reportedly included wrongfully accused people, causing them to be deported without an appeal process or seeing their incriminating evidence.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A testing company examiner who accused thousands of past test takers of cheating on flawed voice-matching evidence, leading the government to deport them without seeing that evidence.
Civil laws: Defamation (libel and slander) (Restatement (Second) of Torts § 558; Walters v. OpenAI, L.L.C., No. 23-A-04860-2 (Ga. Super. Ct. Gwinnett Cnty. May 19, 2025)); Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7); Administrative Procedure Act review (5 U.S.C. §§ 702, 706(2)(A)-(B))
How the company is reached: As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Barriers to liability: Government immunity, Outside US reach, No private right of action
Human precedent for each law: VS-DEFAMATION: K-Mart Corp. v. Washington, 866 P.2d 274 (Nev. 1993) [Liability found]; VF-APA: Wagafe v. Biden, 764 F. Supp. 3d 980 (W.D. Wash. 2025) [Liability found]
Reasoning note: ETS's false cheating accusations may be defamatory but likely privileged. Deporting people without showing them the evidence is a due process challenge to a federal agency under the APA, without damages (D-BIVENS).

Title: Facebook’s Hate Speech Detection Algorithms Allegedly Disproportionately Failed to Remove Racist Content towards Minority Groups
Description: Facebook’s hate-speech detection algorithms was found by company researchers to have under-reported less common but more harmful content that was more often experienced by minority groups such as Black, Muslim, LGBTQ, and Jewish users.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A platform's moderators who missed most of the rarer but more harmful racist posts aimed at Black, Muslim, LGBTQ, and Jewish users.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Barriers to liability: Section 230, First Amendment, No duty owed
Gap note: No US law requires platforms to remove hate speech posted by users, and section 230 bars claims for failing to do so.
Reasoning note: Uneven enforcement against third-party content is not a denial of service on a protected basis under public accommodation law.

Title: Facebook "News Feed" Allegedly Boosted Misinformation and Violating Content Following Use of MSI Metric
Description: After the “News Feed” algorithm had been overhauled to boost engagement between friends and family in early 2018, its heavy weighting of re-shared content was alleged found by company researchers to have pushed content creators to reorient their posts towards outrage and sensationalism, causing a proliferation of misinformation, toxicity, and violent content.
Who did the harm: How the system was built, trained, or marketed
If a human did it: A newspaper editor who rewarded writers for outrage-bait by giving the most inflammatory and misleading pieces the front page.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Ranking choices that amplify sensational and misleading posts are editorial judgments protected by the First Amendment and section 230; no US law reaches them.
Reasoning note: No identifiable person is tied to a specific harm; amplification of third-party content is a design choice without a legal duty.
MIT risk subdomain: 3.2 Pollution of information ecosystem and loss of consensus reality

Title: Image Upscaling Algorithm PULSE Allegedly Produced Facial Images with Caucasian Features More Often
Description: Image upscaling tool PULSE powered by NVIDIA's StyleGAN reportedly generated faces with Caucasian features more often, although AI academics, engineers, and researchers were not in agreement about where the source of bias was.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
If a human did it: A sketch artist who, asked to sharpen blurry photos, tended to draw everyone with white features, without targeting anyone.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Biased output of a research tool, with no targeted person and no denied service, is not unlawful.
Reasoning note: A research demo producing skewed images harms no identifiable person.

Title: Networking Platform Giggle Employs AI to Determine Users’ Gender, Allegedly Excluding Transgender Women
Description: A social networking platform, Giggle, allegedly collected, shared to third-parties, and used sensitive information and biometric data to verify whether a person is a woman via facial recognition, which critics claimed to be discriminatory against women of color and harmful towards trans women.
Harmed parties: women-of-color, trans-women, women-and-girls, women, privacy, biometric-data-subjects
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
Secondary structure: How the system was built, trained, or marketed
If a human did it: A women-only club doorman who judged from applicants' faces whether they were women, turned away trans women, and passed their photos to an outside firm.
Civil law codes: VS-STATE-CIVIL-RIGHTS, VS-UNRUH-DPA, VS-BIPA, VS-BIOMETRIC-STATE, VS-CCPA, VS-PRIVACY-TORTS
Civil laws: State anti-discrimination statutes (Cal. Gov. Code § 12940 (FEHA); Cal. Civ. Code § 51 (Unruh Act); N.Y. Exec. Law § 296); California Unruh Civil Rights Act and Disabled Persons Act (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 51(b), (f), 52(a), 54.1, 54.3; Munson v. Del Taco, Inc., 46 Cal. 4th 661, 670 (2009)); Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (740 ILCS 14/15, 14/20); Texas and Washington biometric identifier laws (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 503.001; Wash. Rev. Code § 19.375.020); California Consumer Privacy Act / CPRA (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1798.100-1798.199.100); Invasion of privacy torts (Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 652B-652E)
Preventive rules: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (740 ILCS 14/15, 14/20); Texas and Washington biometric identifier laws (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 503.001; Wash. Rev. Code § 19.375.020); FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty; As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Human precedent for each law: VS-PRIVACY-TORTS: In re Facebook, Inc. Internet Tracking Litigation, 956 F.3d 589 (9th Cir. 2020) [Claim allowed to proceed]; RF-FTC5: Federal Trade Commission v. Rite Aid Corporation, No. 2:23-cv-05023 (E.D. Pa.), Stipulated Order for Permanent Injunction, ECF No. 19 (signed Feb. 23, 2024; entered Feb. 26, 2024) [Consent order]; VS-STATE-CIVIL-RIGHTS: Candelore v. Tinder, Inc., 19 Cal. App. 5th 1138 (2018) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-BIPA: Deyerler v. HireVue, Inc., No. 1:22-cv-01284 (N.D. Ill. Feb. 26, 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-BIOMETRIC-STATE: State of Texas v. Google LLC (Texas Attorney General CUBI action, Midland County), Civil enforcement action in Midland County under Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 503.001 and the DTPA (cause number not shown in the sources read), described in In re Google, LLC, 705 S.W.3d 479 (Tex. App. 2025) (No. 15-24-00090-CV, orig. proceeding); later resolved in the AG's $1.375 billion settlement with Google [Consent order]; VS-UNRUH-DPA: Candelore v. Tinder, Inc., 19 Cal. App. 5th 1138 (2018) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: No federal public accommodation law covers sex, so state law carries the exclusion; California's Unruh Act bars sex and gender identity discrimination by any business. Biometric claims need Illinois, Texas, Washington, or California users.

Title: Researchers' Homosexual-Men Detection Model Denounced as a Threat to LGBTQ People's Safety and Privacy
Description: Researchers at Stanford Graduate School of Business developed a model that determined, on a binary scale, whether someone was homosexual using only his facial image, which advocacy groups such as GLAAD and the Human Rights Campaign denounced as flawed science and threatening to LGBTQ folks.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
Secondary structure: How the system was built, trained, or marketed
If a human did it: A researcher who published a method claiming to tell from photos whether men are gay, without identifying or outing anyone.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Publishing contested research on inferring sexual orientation, without exposing any individual, is protected speech; no US law reaches it.
Reasoning note: The threat is prospective misuse; the record shows no person identified or harmed and no unlawful data collection.
MIT risk subdomain: 2.1 Compromise of privacy by obtaining, leaking or correctly inferring sensitive information

Title: Collaborative Filtering Prone to Popularity Bias, Resulting in Overrepresentation of Popular Items in the Recommendation Outputs
Description: Collaborative filtering prone to popularity bias, resulting in overrepresentation of popular items in the recommendation outputs.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
If a human did it: A shop assistant who kept recommending the bestsellers over lesser-known items, harming no one in particular.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Popularity bias in recommendations is a quality issue, not a legal wrong; no law requires balanced recommendations.
Reasoning note: Generic technical phenomenon with no identified victim or protected-class denial.

Title: Facebook Allegedly Failed to Police Anti-Rohingya Hate Speech Content That Contributed to Violence in Myanmar
Description: Facebook allegedly did not adequately remove anti-Rohingya hate speech, some of which was extremely violent and dehumanizing, on its platform, contributing to the violence faced by Rohingya communities in Myanmar.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A bulletin board owner who left up posts inciting violence against an ethnic minority while that violence was happening.
Civil laws: Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7); Wrongful death and survival actions (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 377.60; Fla. Stat. §§ 768.16-.26)
How the company is reached: As maker of a defective product
If the AI were a legal person: Section 230 question, same either way (company recommended others' content)
Barriers to liability: Section 230, Causation, Outside US reach, First Amendment
Reasoning note: Negligence for failing to curb incitement that contributed to deaths fits in principle, but section 230 bars claims treating the platform as publisher of users' posts; accomplice crimes need intent.
MIT risk subdomain: 4.1 Disinformation, surveillance, and influence at scale

Title: Target Suggested Maternity-Related Advertisements to a Teenage Girl's Home, Allegedly Correctly Predicting Her Pregnancy via Algorithm
Description: Target recommended maternity-related items to a family in Atlanta via ads, allegedly predicting their teenage daughter’s pregnancy before her father did, although critics have called into question the predictability of the algorithm and the authenticity of its claims.
Who did the harm: How the system was built, trained, or marketed
If a human did it: A store marketer who studied a teenager's purchases, guessed she was pregnant, and mailed baby-product ads to her family's home.
Civil laws: Invasion of privacy torts (Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 652B-652E); California Consumer Privacy Act / CPRA (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1798.100-1798.199.100); Washington My Health My Data Act (Wash. Rev. Code §§ 19.373.030, 19.373.090)
Preventive rules: FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45); Washington My Health My Data Act (Wash. Rev. Code §§ 19.373.030, 19.373.090)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Human precedent for each law: VS-PRIVACY-TORTS: In re Facebook, Inc. Internet Tracking Litigation, 956 F.3d 589 (9th Cir. 2020) [Claim allowed to proceed]; RF-FTC5: Federal Trade Commission v. Kochava, Inc., 715 F. Supp. 3d 1319 (D. Idaho 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-CCPA: People v. General Motors (California Attorney General settlement), California Superior Court civil enforcement action; complaint and settlement announced May 8, 2026; the AG's release links a court-approved amended judgment dated June 30, 2026 (case number not stated on the AG release) [Consent order]
Reasoning note: Inferring pregnancy from purchases is lawful in most states, but Washington treats algorithmic health inferences as consumer health data needing consent; private-facts claims need wider publicity, and the story's accuracy is disputed.
MIT risk subdomain: 2.1 Compromise of privacy by obtaining, leaking or correctly inferring sensitive information

Title: Traffic Camera Misread Text on Pedestrian's Shirt as License Plate, Causing UK Officials to Issue Fine to an Unrelated Person
Description: A Bath resident was wrongly fined by the local officials because an automated license plate recognition camera misread the text on her shirt as a license plate number.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A traffic warden who misread the writing on a pedestrian's shirt as a license plate and fined an unrelated car owner.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: A mistaken ticket that can be contested breaches no US law; an available appeal satisfies due process.
Reasoning note: A one-off clerical-type error by a government agency with an appeal route supports no damages claim.

Title: NarxCare’s Risk Score Model Allegedly Lacked Validation and Trained on Data with High Risk of Bias
Description: NarxCare's overdose risk algorithm, lacking peer-reviewed validation, uses sensitive data like doctor visits, prescriptions, and possibly genetic information, leading to significant biases against women and Black patients. Factors like sexual abuse and criminal records exacerbate stigmas and disparities, often resulting in unjust denial of necessary pain medication. The newly approved AvertD genetic test shares similar issues, further complicating and potentially harming medical treatment decisions.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A pharmacy consultant who flagged patients as likely drug misusers from unvalidated factors like past sexual abuse, so women and Black patients were more often denied pain medication.
Civil law codes: VF-ADA3, VS-UNRUH-DPA, VF-504, VF-ACA1557, VS-STATE-CIVIL-RIGHTS, VS-NEGLIGENCE
Civil laws: ADA Title III (public accommodations) (42 U.S.C. § 12182); California Unruh Civil Rights Act and Disabled Persons Act (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 51(b), (f), 52(a), 54.1, 54.3; Munson v. Del Taco, Inc., 46 Cal. 4th 661, 670 (2009)); Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794); ACA section 1557 (discrimination in health programs) (42 U.S.C. § 18116(a)); State anti-discrimination statutes (Cal. Gov. Code § 12940 (FEHA); Cal. Civ. Code § 51 (Unruh Act); N.Y. Exec. Law § 296); Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7)
Preventive rules: FDA medical device premarket review (incl. software as a medical device) (21 U.S.C. §§ 360(k), 360c, 360e); Colorado automated decision-making technology law (SB 26-189, replacing the 2024 Colorado AI Act) (Colo. S.B. 26-189 (2026), repealing and reenacting S.B. 24-205); FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45); Section 1557 rule on patient care decision support tools (45 C.F.R. § 92.210 (89 Fed. Reg. 37692 (May 6, 2024)))
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty; As maker of a defective product
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Human precedent for each law: VS-NEGLIGENCE: Taylor v. Intuitive Surgical, Inc., 187 Wash. 2d 743, 389 P.3d 517 (2017) [Claim allowed to proceed]; RF-FTC5: Federal Trade Commission v. Rite Aid Corporation, No. 2:23-cv-05023 (E.D. Pa.), Stipulated Order for Permanent Injunction, ECF No. 19 (signed Feb. 23, 2024; entered Feb. 26, 2024) [Consent order]; VS-STATE-CIVIL-RIGHTS: Louis v. SafeRent Solutions, LLC, 685 F. Supp. 3d 19 (D. Mass. 2023) [Claim allowed to proceed]; RF-FDA-DEVICE: United States v. Facteau, 89 F.4th 1 (1st Cir. 2023) [Conviction]; VS-UNRUH-DPA: Candelore v. Tinder, Inc., 19 Cal. App. 5th 1138 (2018) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VF-504: Pushkin v. Regents of the University of Colorado, 658 F.2d 1372 (10th Cir. 1981) [Liability found]; VF-ADA3: Bragdon v. Abbott, 524 U.S. 624 (1998) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: Providers and pharmacies using scores that deny care to disabled patients face ADA, Unruh, 504, and Section 1557 claims; Section 1557 race claims need intent. The vendor faces negligence; disparities need proof.

Title: AI Tools Failed to Sufficiently Predict COVID Patients, Some Potentially Harmful
Description: AI tools failed to sufficiently predict COVID patients, some potentially harmful.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
If a human did it: A team of researchers who published COVID diagnosis rules that did not work, with no specific patient shown to be harmed.
Preventive rules: FDA medical device premarket review (incl. software as a medical device) (21 U.S.C. §§ 360(k), 360c, 360e)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Gap note: No identified patient harm; the only hook is premarket review for diagnostic software.
Reasoning note: Thin record: inaccurate prediction tools with only potential harm; clinical use would need FDA clearance as device software.

Title: Fake LinkedIn Profiles Created Using GAN Photos
Description: More than a thousand inauthentic LinkedIn profiles using allegedly GAN-generated photos were notified by researchers at Stanford to LinkedIn’s staff, and many of which were removed for violating rules against creating fake profiles and falsifying information.
Who did the harm: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A marketer who created over a thousand fake LinkedIn profiles with invented faces and false credentials.
Civil laws: State unfair and deceptive practices laws (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17200, 17500; Fla. Stat. § 501.204; Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46); Breach of contract and warranty (U.C.C. §§ 2-313, 2-314 (e.g., Cal. Com. Code §§ 2313, 2314))
Preventive rules: FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45)
How the company is reached: Only as supplier of a misused tool
If the AI were a legal person: Same either way: company only supplied a tool a person misused
Human precedent for each law: RF-FTC5: Federal Trade Commission v. LeadClick Media, LLC, 838 F.3d 158 (2d Cir. 2016) [Liability found]; VS-UDAP: Dorsey v. Rockhard Laboratories, LLC, No. 2:13-cv-07557 (C.D. Cal. Sept. 19, 2014) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-WARRANTY-CONTRACT: Ticketmaster L.L.C. v. RMG Technologies, Inc., 507 F. Supp. 2d 1096 (C.D. Cal. 2007) [Preliminary injunction]
Reasoning note: Fake personas without impersonating a real person or a shown fraud are not crimes; deceptive commercial use and breach of the platform's terms depend on how the profiles were used.

Title: Cruise Autonomous Taxi Allegedly Bolted off from Police After Being Pulled over in San Francisco
Description: An autonomous Chevy Bolt operated by Cruise was pulled over in San Francisco, and as the police attempted to engage with the car, it reportedly bolted off, pulled over again, and put on its hazards lights on at a point farther down the road.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A driver who, when police stopped him, drove forward a short distance and pulled over again with hazard lights on.
Preventive rules: California autonomous vehicle testing and deployment rules (Cal. Veh. Code § 38750; Cal. Code Regs. tit. 13, § 228.00 et seq.)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Gap note: Moving a short way after a stop and stopping again harmed no one; fleeing police (CS-TRAFFIC-CRIMES) needs intent to evade, so only California's AV permit rules apply.
Human precedent for each law: RS-AV-PERMIT: California DMV investigation of Cruise LLC and 50% fleet reduction (August 2023), Cal. Dep't of Motor Vehicles, Cruise LLC fleet reduction during investigation (Aug. 2023), as recorded in Cal. Assembly Comm. on Transportation, Informational Hearing Background Paper (June 8, 2026) [Regulatory action]
Reasoning note: The car stopped again with hazards on, which shows no intent to evade; no injury or property damage.

Title: Starship’s Autonomous Food Delivery Robot Allegedly Stranded at Railroad Crossing in Oregon, Run over by Freight Train
Description: A Starship food delivery robot deployed by Oregon State University reportedly failed to cross the railroad, becoming stranded, and ending up being struck by an oncoming freight train.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
Secondary structure: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A courier who got a delivery cart stuck on a railroad crossing, where a freight train destroyed it, injuring no one.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Only the deployer's own robot was destroyed and no one was hurt; no law is implicated on these facts.
Reasoning note: A near miss for the train crew; a small cart posed little derailment risk, so endangerment does not fit.

Title: Google’s Assistive Writing Feature Provided Allegedly Unnecessary and Clumsy Suggestions
Description: Google’s “inclusive language” feature prompting writers to consider alternatives to non-inclusive words reportedly also recommend alternatives for words such as “landlord” and “motherboard,” which critics said was a form of obtrusive, unnecessary, and bias-reinforcing speech-policing.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
If a human did it: An editor who suggested replacing words like landlord and motherboard with alternatives, annoying writers but harming no one.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Unwanted writing suggestions are not a legal harm; no law is implicated.
Reasoning note: Users remained free to ignore the suggestions.

Title: Tesla Owner Activated "Smart Summon" Feature, Causing a Collision with an Aircraft in a Washington Airport
Description: A Tesla Model Y was shown on video slowly crashing into a Vision Jet in Spokane, Washington, allegedly due to its owner activating the “Smart Summon” feature.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A valet who slowly drove a customer's car into a parked private jet at an airport.
Civil laws: Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7); Product liability: design defect and failure to warn (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability §§ 1, 2; Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., 785 F. Supp. 3d 1157 (M.D. Fla. 2025))
Preventive rules: Motor vehicle safety standards, defect recalls, crash reporting (49 U.S.C. §§ 30112, 30118-30120, 30165; NHTSA Standing General Order 2021-01)
How the company is reached: As maker of a defective product; As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Human precedent for each law: VS-NEGLIGENCE: Hoeben v. FCA US LLC, 2026 NY Slip Op 05238 (App. Div. 1st Dep't 2026) (Index No. 153682/18; Appeal No. 6709) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-PRODUCTS: Benavides v. Tesla, Inc., No. 1:21-cv-21940-BB (S.D. Fla. Feb. 19, 2026) (order denying Tesla's amended renewed motion for judgment as a matter of law or new trial); final judgment entered Aug. 3, 2025 [Liability found]; RF-NHTSA: Tesla, Inc., Safety Recall 23V-085 (Full Self-Driving Beta may act unsafely around intersections), NHTSA Recall No. 23V-085, Part 573 Safety Recall Report (submitted Feb. 15, 2023) [Safety recall]
Reasoning note: Driving into a parked aircraft states a negligence claim for the jet's damage; accidental property damage is not a crime. Liability splits between the owner who activated it and the maker.

Title: DALL-E 2 Reported for Gender and Racially Biased Outputs
Description: Developers of OpenAI's DALL-E 2 cited risks of the model, varying from misuse as disinformation and explicit content generation, to gender and racial bias.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
If a human did it: An illustrator who disclosed that his work tends to reflect gender and racial stereotypes, without targeting anyone.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Developer-disclosed bias risks with no targeted person are protected expression; no law is implicated.
Reasoning note: Risk documentation by the developer, not a realized harm to any person.

Title: Algorithm Used by the Malaysian Judiciary Reportedly Recommended Unusually High Sentencing to a Drug Possession Case
Description: The AI system used by the Malaysian judiciary which explicitly considered age, employment, and socio-economic data provided sentencing to a drug possession case that was alleged by lawyer to be disproportionately high for the crime committed.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A sentencing judge who gave an unusually harsh drug-possession sentence after weighing the defendant's age, job, and income.
Preventive rules: Judicial competence duty (ABA Model Code of Judicial Conduct Rule 2.5(A) (as adopted by states))
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Gap note: Sentencing errors are corrected on appeal and judges have absolute immunity from damages; the only hook is the judicial competence duty, enforced through discipline.
Human precedent for each law: RF-JUDICIAL-CONDUCT: In re Disciplinary Proceeding Against Flood, 5 Wn.3d 673 (Wash. 2025) (en banc) [Sanction]
Reasoning note: A judge who adopts an AI sentencing recommendation without independent review risks breaching the competence duty; weighing socioeconomic factors may support due process or equal protection arguments on appeal, not damages.

Title: BMW Sedan Made a Prohibited Left Turn, Colliding with a Cruise Autonomous Vehicle
Description: A BMW Sedan reportedly made an illegal left turn, causing a minor collision but no injuries with a Cruise autonomous vehicle (AV) operating in autonomous mode.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
If a human did it: A driver whose car was hit by another driver making an illegal left turn, with minor damage and no injuries.

Title: IRS Audited Black Taxpayers More Frequently Reportedly Due to Algorithm
Description: The IRS was auditing Black taxpayers more frequently than other groups allegedly due to the design of their algorithms, focusing on easier-to-conduct audits which inadvertently correlated with the group's pattern of tax filing errors.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A federal tax office that chose to prioritize the simplest audits, which without intending it fell far more often on Black taxpayers.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Barriers to liability: Government immunity, Mental state, No private right of action
Gap note: Unintended racial disparity by a federal agency is not actionable: equal protection requires intent, section 1983 does not reach federal actors, and Title VI covers only federally funded recipients.
Reasoning note: Inadvertent disparate impact in federal audit selection falls between library hooks: VF-APA review is likely unavailable because audit selection is committed to agency discretion, equal protection needs intent, and Bivens damages are barred (D-BIVENS).

Title: AI-Produced Livestream Sitcom Received Temporary Twitch Ban for Transphobic Segment

How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Offensive comedy that targets no individual is protected speech; the platform's temporary ban is its own policy, not a legal consequence.
Reasoning note: Offensive output with no targeted person.

Title: Apple Devices Mistook Skiing Activities, Dialed False Distress Emergency Calls
Description: Apple devices of skiers and snowboarders reportedly misclassified winter activities as accidents, which resulted in numerous false inadvertent distress calls to 911 dispatchers.

If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Good-faith mistaken emergency calls are not false reports, and dispatch burdens are public costs that agencies generally cannot recover in tort.
Reasoning note: False-report crimes require knowledge that the emergency is false; the device's misclassification carries no such knowledge.

Title: ChatGPT Provided Non-Existent Citations and Links when Prompted by Users
Description: When prompted about providing references, ChatGPT was reportedly generating non-existent but convincing-looking citations and links, which is also known as "hallucination".

Reasoning note: General hallucination phenomenon with no specific victim; downstream misuse by lawyers is coded as a person using AI as the tool.

Title: Private Medical Photos Were Reportedly Found in LAION-5B AI Training Dataset
Description: In September 2022, an artist using the name Lapine reported finding private post-operative medical photos of herself in LAION-5B, a web-scraped image-text dataset used in AI image-synthesis research. Ars Technica confirmed her images were referenced in the dataset and reported finding thousands of similar patient medical-record photos.

If a human did it: A dataset compiler who scraped the web and included links to thousands of patients' private post-operative medical photos in a widely shared research collection.
Civil laws: Invasion of privacy torts (Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 652B-652E); Washington My Health My Data Act (Wash. Rev. Code §§ 19.373.030, 19.373.090)
Preventive rules: HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules (45 C.F.R. pts. 160, 164); FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45); California Consumer Privacy Act / CPRA (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1798.100-1798.199.100); Washington My Health My Data Act (Wash. Rev. Code §§ 19.373.030, 19.373.090)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Human precedent for each law: VS-PRIVACY-TORTS: In re Facebook, Inc. Internet Tracking Litigation, 956 F.3d 589 (9th Cir. 2020) [Claim allowed to proceed]; RF-FTC5: Federal Trade Commission v. Kochava, Inc., 715 F. Supp. 3d 1319 (D. Idaho 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-CCPA: People v. (HHS OCR Resolution Agreement and Corrective Action Plan), HHS Office for Civil Rights resolution agreement effective Mar. 17, 2023 (announced May 16, 2023) [Consent order]
Reasoning note: HIPAA binds the provider whose records leaked, not the scrapers; Washington's health data law requires consent to collect or share such photos, though compilers argue they only indexed images already online.
MIT risk subdomain: 2.1 Compromise of privacy by obtaining, leaking or correctly inferring sensitive information

Title: AI-Generated Text Detectors Reportedly Misclassified Human and AI-Written Text

OpenAI said its classifier identified only 26% of AI-written samples as likely AI-written and falsely labeled 9% of human-written text.

If a human did it: A grader who claimed to spot ghostwritten essays but missed most of them and wrongly flagged some genuine work, in public tests where no student was punished.
Preventive rules: FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45)
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Inaccurate detectors harm no one until a school disciplines a student on a false positive; overstated accuracy claims are the only hook.

Title: Google's Bard Shared Factually Inaccurate Info in Promo Video

Gap note: An erroneous fact in a product demo is not a misstatement about the company's business, and stock losses from a revealed product flaw are not actionable without scienter.

Title: Facebook Allegedly Failed to Police Hate Speech Content That Contributed to Ethnic Violence in Ethiopia
Description: Facebook allegedly did not adequately remove hate speech, some of which was extremely violent and dehumanizing, on its platform including through automated means, contributing to the violence faced by ethnic communities in Ethiopia.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A publisher's moderators who left up violent, dehumanizing posts against ethnic groups in local languages while ethnic violence spread.
Civil laws: Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7); Wrongful death and survival actions (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 377.60; Fla. Stat. §§ 768.16-.26)
How the company is reached: As principal or employer (agency); As maker of a defective product
If the AI were a legal person: Section 230 question, same either way (company recommended others' content)
Barriers to liability: Section 230, Causation, No duty owed, Outside US reach
Gap note: Section 230 and Twitter v. Taamneh make claims for failing to remove third-party incitement nearly impossible in the US, despite deaths.
Reasoning note: Accessory crimes need knowing, substantial assistance to specific attacks, not shown. Negligence fits conceptually, but duty, causation, and section 230 defeat it under current law.

Title: Tesla FSD Reportedly Increased Crash Risk, Prompting Recall

Title: Cruise Robotaxi Initially Blamed for Ambulance Delay in Case Where Patient Later Died; Subsequent Reports Clear Cruise of Fault

Despite this, the incident is included as it highlights challenges in the interaction between autonomous vehicles and emergency services in urban settings.

Title: Chatbot Encourages Man to Plot Assassination of Queen Elizabeth II
Description: In 2021, Jaswant Singh Chail was urged by a Replika chatbot to assassinate Queen Elizabeth II. Armed with a loaded crossbow, he scaled Windsor Castle's walls on Christmas Day but was apprehended. Motivated by the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre, Chail intended to kill the monarch. The chatbot had affirmed his plans. He was sentenced to nine years in prison in 2023.

If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent

Real-world action reported: Chail sentenced to nine years in prison (2023)

Reasoning note: Soliciting or counseling a murder is criminal only with intent that it occur; the bot's affirmation shows encouragement but not intent. No one but the attacker was physically harmed, so no civil claim.

If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
