Reasoning note: Gender-skewed delivery of job ads is a reported disparate outcome; whether the platform is covered as an employment agency or aider under state law is the open question.

Title: Google Ads Allegedly Serving Content on AI-Generated Misinformation Sites
Description: Google’s advertising platform, Google Ads, has allegedly been found to be serving ads on AI-generated content farms that often disseminate misinformation. Despite policies prohibiting such practices, reportedly there are approximately 356 out of 393 ads from major brands that were found to be served by Google on these problematic sites. Particularly concerning according to the reporting were instances where Google Ads were found on sites like MedicalOutline.com, which spreads harmful health misinformation.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: An ad broker who placed major brands' ads on misinformation sites despite promising not to.
Civil laws: Breach of contract and warranty (U.C.C. §§ 2-313, 2-314 (e.g., Cal. Com. Code §§ 2313, 2314))
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Gap note: Funding misinformation sites is not unlawful; the only hook is advertisers' contract terms if they promise policy-compliant placement.
Human precedent for each law: VS-WARRANTY-CONTRACT: RRX Industries, Inc. v. Lab-Con, Inc., 772 F.2d 543 (9th Cir. 1985) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: Brands may have contract claims if placement violated agreed terms; the public harm from monetized misinformation has no legal remedy.

Title: Racial Bias in Lung Function Diagnostic Algorithm Leads to Underdiagnosis in Black Men
Description: A study published in JAMA Network Open reveals that racial bias built into a commonly used medical diagnostic algorithm for lung function may be leading to underdiagnoses of breathing problems in Black men. The study suggests that as many as 40% more Black male patients might have been accurately diagnosed if the software were not racially biased. The software algorithm adjusts diagnostic thresholds based on race, affecting medical treatments and interventions.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A hospital lung specialist who applied a stricter diagnostic threshold to Black men than to white men because of their race, so fewer Black men were diagnosed with breathing problems.
Civil laws: ACA section 1557 (discrimination in health programs) (42 U.S.C. § 18116(a)); State anti-discrimination statutes (Cal. Gov. Code § 12940 (FEHA); Cal. Civ. Code § 51 (Unruh Act); N.Y. Exec. Law § 296); Professional negligence (medical, legal, other licensed professions) (Common law; e.g., Cal. Civ. Code § 3333.2 (medical damages cap))
Preventive rules: Section 1557 rule on patient care decision support tools (45 C.F.R. § 92.210 (89 Fed. Reg. 37692 (May 6, 2024)))
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Human precedent for each law: VS-STATE-CIVIL-RIGHTS: Louis v. SafeRent Solutions, LLC, 685 F. Supp. 3d 19 (D. Mass. 2023) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-MALPRACTICE: Gapinski v. Gujrati, 2017 IL App (3d) 150502, 77 N.E.3d 1148 [Liability found]
Reasoning note: An explicit race-based threshold is facial race discrimination, meeting the intent that private Section 1557 claims need; the 2024 tool rule covers race inputs. Malpractice is weak because race correction was standard care.

Title: Instagram Algorithms Allegedly Promote Accounts Facilitating Child Sex Abuse Content
Description: An investigation disclosed that Instagram's recommendation algorithms are promoting accounts that facilitate and sell child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The study, conducted by The Wall Street Journal and researchers at Stanford University and the University of Massachusetts Amherst, indicates that Instagram's algorithms not only allow for the discovery of such accounts through keyword searches but also actively recommend them to users within the network. The issue is especially concerning given Instagram's popularity among teenagers.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A social club host who steered members, including teenagers, toward people selling child sexual abuse material.
Crime if a human did it: Yes, if the required mental state is shown
Criminal laws: Child sexual abuse material (incl. morphed images of identifiable minors) (18 U.S.C. §§ 2252A, 2256(8)); Aiding and abetting; principal liability (18 U.S.C. § 2)
Civil laws: Civil remedy for victims of child sexual exploitation (18 U.S.C. § 2255); Product liability: design defect and failure to warn (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability §§ 1, 2; Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., 785 F. Supp. 3d 1157 (M.D. Fla. 2025)); Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7)
Preventive rules: Provider duty to report child sexual abuse material (18 U.S.C. §§ 2258A(a), (e), 2258B)
How the company is reached: As maker of a defective product; As principal or employer (agency); Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Section 230 question, same either way (company recommended others' content)
Human precedent for each law: VS-NEGLIGENCE: Anderson v. TikTok, Inc., 116 F.4th 180 (3d Cir. 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-PRODUCTS: Anderson v. TikTok, Inc., 116 F.4th 180 (3d Cir. 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; CF-CSAM: United States v. Williams, 553 U.S. 285, 128 S. Ct. 1830 (2008) [Conviction]; VF-CSAM-CIVIL: Jane Doe #1 v. MG Freesites, Ltd., 676 F. Supp. 3d 1136 (N.D. Ala. 2022) [Claim allowed to proceed]; CF-AID: United States v. Noxon, No. 07-40152-01-RDR (D. Kan. Oct. 28, 2008) (order recording sentencing rulings) [Conviction]; RF-NCMEC-REPORT: Doe 1 v. Twitter, Inc., 148 F.4th 635 (9th Cir. 2025) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: Aiding CSAM distribution requires knowing the recommended accounts sold CSAM; recommendations are the company's own conduct, but courts often treat them as publishing third-party content under section 230.

Title: Illinois Residents File Class Action Lawsuit Against Facial Recognition Technology Companies for Allegedly Violating BIPA
Description: A class action lawsuit was filed against several facial recognition technology companies for allegedly violating the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA). The defendants are accused of offering a facial recognition search engine called Pimeyes, which collects images from databases across the internet and scans them into their database seemingly without consent. This action is claimed to invade the privacy of millions of Americans. The lawsuit argues that Pimeyes lacks publicly available policies regarding data storage and deletion, in contravention of BIPA's requirements for informed written consent before collecting biometric data.
Alleged deployers: transaction-cloud, public-mirror, pimeyes, lukasz-kowalczyk, giorgi-gobronidze, face-recognition-solutions, emea-robotics, does-125, denis-tatina, carribex
Alleged developers: transaction-cloud, public-mirror, pimeyes, lukasz-kowalczyk, giorgi-gobronidze, face-recognition-solutions, emea-robotics, does-1-25, denis-tatina, carribex, surveillance-technology-developers, facial-recognition-system-developers
Harmed parties: nicholas-clayton, misty-mcgraw, manuel-clayton, illinois-residents, amy-newton, amanda-curry, general-public, general-public-of-illinois, privacy, biometric-data-subjects
Who did the harm: How the system was built, trained, or marketed
If a human did it: A face-search business that copied people's photos from across the internet and built faceprints of them without notice, consent, or a retention policy.
Civil laws: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (740 ILCS 14/15, 14/20); Invasion of privacy torts (Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 652B-652E); Texas and Washington biometric identifier laws (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 503.001; Wash. Rev. Code § 19.375.020)
Preventive rules: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (740 ILCS 14/15, 14/20); FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Real-world action reported: Illinois residents filed BIPA class action against PimEyes operators

Kochava, Inc., 715 F. Supp. 3d 1319 (D. Idaho 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-BIPA: Patel v. Facebook, Inc., 932 F.3d 1264 (9th Cir. 2019) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-BIOMETRIC-STATE: State of Texas v. Meta Platforms, Inc. (Texas Attorney General CUBI action and settlement), Texas Attorney General civil enforcement action under Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 503.001 and the DTPA, filed February 2022 (trial court cause number not shown in the sources read); settled for $1.4 billion. Title: Kremlin-Linked Entities Allegedly Using Generative AI to Spread Russian Disinformation in Latin America
Description: Moscow-based tech firms and an industry association with links to the Kremlin are allegedly using generative AI to spread Russian disinformation in countries throughout Central America and South America. According to the U.S. Department of State, the Russian companies rely on local writers to compose stories which are then amplified across social media using artificial intelligence chatbots.
Alleged deployers: structura-national-technologies, social-design-agency, oleg-yasinsky, oleg-yasinskiy, nikolay-tupikin, institute-for-internet-development, ilya-gambashidze, andrey-perla
Who did the harm: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A foreign propaganda firm that hired local writers and used fake accounts to spread state disinformation across Latin American media.
Crime if a human did it: Yes, if the required mental state is shown
Criminal laws: Foreign Agents Registration Act (22 U.S.C. §§ 612(a), 614, 618(a)); Acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government (18 U.S.C. § 951(a))
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off

Human precedent for each law: CF-951: United States v. Sun (Yaoning Sun), No. 2:24-cr-00777-RGK-1 (C.D. Cal. Feb. 10, 2026) (judgment) [Conviction]; CF-FARA: RM Broadcasting, LLC v. U.S. Department of Justice, 379 F. Supp. 3d 1256 (S.D. Fla. 2019) [Liability found]

Title: FTC Targets Edmodo for Unlawful Use of Children’s Data and Delegating Compliance to Schools
Description: Edmodo, an education technology provider, violated the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act Rule (COPPA Rule) by collecting and using children's personal data for advertising purposes without parental consent, according to the FTC. The company outsourced its compliance responsibilities to schools, thereby making them "solely" responsible for COPPA compliance without adequate disclosure. Edmodo is facing a proposed order prohibiting such practices, marking a precedent in the ed tech industry.
Harmed parties: teachers, students, schools-and-teachers-who-were-misinformed-and-burdened-with-coppa-compliance-responsibilities-without-adequate-disclosure, minors, educational-communities, children-whose-data-was-collected-and-used-for-advertising, biometric-data-subjects, privacy

Preventive rules: Children's Online Privacy Protection Act and Rule (15 U.S.C. §§ 6501-6506; 16 C.F.R. pt. 312); FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45); Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (20 U.S.C. § 1232g; 34 C.F.R. pt. 99)

Title: Apparent Failure to Accurately Label Primates in Image Recognition Software Due to Alleged Fear of Racial Bias
Description: Eight years after Google Photos mislabeled images of Black individuals as "gorillas," image recognition software by Google, Apple, Amazon, and Microsoft still shows signs of either avoiding or inaccurately categorizing primates. Tests reveal that Google and Apple Photos refrain from labeling primates altogether, possibly to avoid the risk of perpetuating racial stereotypes. Microsoft OneDrive fails to identify any animals, while Amazon Photos overgeneralizes in its labeling.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
If a human did it: A photo-album organizer who refused to label any monkeys or apes in customers' pictures, fearing a past offensive mistake; no one was harmed.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Declining to label animals in photos is a product limitation, not a legal wrong to anyone.
Reasoning note: Test-based reporting of avoidance or overgeneralized labels; no offensive label of a person or denial of service is reported.

Title: Australian Terrorism Prediction Tool Reportedly Disparately Impacts Persons with Autism
Description: An independent report found that the Vera-2R tool, designed to predict the risk of future terrorist activities, considered autism as a risk factor despite lacking empirical evidence to support this claim. The report called into question the tool's overall validity and reliability, stating it was "extremely poor" at accurately predicting risk. The inclusion of autism as a risk factor had potentially serious implications for the tool's use and credibility.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A government risk assessor who rated offenders as likelier future terrorists because they were autistic, using a method shown to predict poorly.
Civil laws: ADA Title II (state and local government) (42 U.S.C. § 12132); Section 1983 (constitutional torts by state actors) (42 U.S.C. § 1983)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Human precedent for each law: VF-1983: Floyd v. City of New York, 959 F. Supp. 2d 540 (S.D.N.Y. 2013) [Liability found]; VF-ADA2: Clark v. Virginia Board of Bar Examiners, 880 F. Supp. 430 (E.D. Va. 1995) [Liability found]
Reasoning note: Treating autism as a risk factor without evidence is disability screening a US public entity could not justify; due process claims arise if invalid scores extended detention, which the record does not detail.

Title: Proliferation of AI-Generated News Websites and Content Farms Across Multiple Languages Degrading Information Integrity
Description: Scores of AI-generated news websites and content farms are producing low-quality, clickbait content in a variety of languages. They are reportedly spreading false information and degrading the quality of information available online. These sites often lack human oversight, feature repetitive language, and sometimes fabricate information, posing a threat to the credibility of online news sources.
Alleged deployers: many, maria-spanadoris, adesh-ingale, getintoknowledge.com, famadillo.com, bestbudgetusa.com, harmonyhustle.com, historyfact.in, countylocalnews.com, tnewsnetwork.com, wavefunction.info, celebritiesdeaths.com, scoopearth.com, filthylucre.com
Who did the harm: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A group of website operators who churned out low-quality clickbait articles, some with made-up facts, to earn ad revenue.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Publishing low-quality or inaccurate content is protected unless it defames an identifiable person or defrauds someone, neither of which the record shows.
Reasoning note: Information-ecosystem harm with no named victim; specific false statements about real people would need to be identified for defamation.
MIT risk subdomain: 3.2 Pollution of information ecosystem and loss of consensus reality

Title: Alleged ChatGPT-Generated Book with a Duplicate Title, Fake Author, and Similar Content Surfaces on Amazon Ahead of Real Author's Book Release
Description: The author Chris Cowell had spent more than a year writing his book "Automating DevOps with GitLab CI/CD Pipelines" when, three weeks before its release, another book appeared bearing the exact title by an author (Marie Karpos) for whom no information could be found. The book appeared to have been written by ChatGPT. While the original Washington Post story does not say so, it is possible the name and description were taken from the Amazon preorder page.
Who did the harm: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A publisher who rushed out a ghostwritten book under a made-up author name with the exact title of another author's forthcoming book, to capture his sales.
Civil laws: Lanham Act false endorsement and false advertising (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)); State unfair and deceptive practices laws (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17200, 17500; Fla. Stat. § 501.204; Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46); Copyright infringement; removal of copyright management information (17 U.S.C. §§ 501, 1202)
How the company is reached: Only as supplier of a misused tool
If the AI were a legal person: Same either way: company only supplied a tool a person misused
Human precedent for each law: VF-LANHAM: Microsoft Corp. v. John Does 1-2, No. 1:24-cv-02719 (D.D.C. Aug. 5, 2026) [Liability found]; VS-UDAP: Dorsey v. Goldsmith, 598 U.S. 508 (2023) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: Single-work titles are protectable only with secondary meaning, hard before release; copyright applies only if the description or text was copied, which the record calls merely possible.
MIT risk subdomain: 6.3 Economic and cultural devaluation of human effort

Title: Cigna Algorithm PXDX Allegedly Rejected Thousands of Patient Claims En Masse in Breach of California Law
Description: Cigna health insurer faces a class-action lawsuit for allegedly using the PXDX ("procedure-to-diagnosis") algorithm to automatically reject over 300,000 patient claims in violation of California law, prompting two members to file the lawsuit seeking damages and a jury trial. Cigna disputes the allegations, claiming the process expedites physician reimbursement and does not result in care denials.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision

Crime if a human did it: Yes, if the required mental state is shown

Stat. § 501.204; Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46); Insurance bad faith (implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing) (Gruenberg v. Aetna Ins. Co., 9 Cal. 3d 566, 575-76 (1973)); ERISA benefit claims, fiduciary duties, and preemption (29 U.S.C. §§ 1104(a)(1), 1132(a)(1)(B), 1144(a); Pilot Life Ins. Co. v. Dedeaux, 481 U.S. 41 (1987))

S.B. 26-189 (2026), repealing and reenacting S.B. 24-205); Unfair claims settlement practices (California) (Cal. Ins. Code § 790.03(h); Moradi-Shalal v. Fireman's Fund Ins. Cos., 46 Cal. 3d 287, 304 (1988))

If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Real-world action reported: Members filed class action against Cigna over PXDX claim rejections

UnitedHealth Group, Inc., 766 F. Supp. 3d 835 (D. Minn. 2025) [Claim allowed to proceed]; RF-INS-UNFAIR: In the Matter of PacifiCare Life and Health Insurance Company (Decision and Order of the Insurance Commissioner), Cal. Dep't of Ins. No. UPA 2007-00004 (Cal. Ins. Comm'r June 9, 2014) (designated precedential), writ granted (Orange Cnty. Super. Ct.), rev'd, PacifiCare Life & Health Ins. Co. v. Lara, No. G056160 (Cal. Ct. App. May 3, 2022) (unpublished); see also PacifiCare Life & Health Ins. Co. v. Jones, 27 Cal. App. 5th 391 (2018) [Regulatory action]; VS-BAD-FAITH: Egan v. Mar. 31, 2025) [Claim allowed to proceed]

Reasoning note: Rejecting claims without the fair review California requires supports bad-faith and contract claims on individual policies; ERISA governs employer plans and preempts those state claims. Fraud needs knowing intent.

Title: Facial Recognition Misidentifies Pregnant Woman Leading to False Arrest in Detroit
Description: Porcha Woodruff was arrested and subsequently had charges dropped due to an unreliable facial recognition match. Despite being visibly pregnant, she was implicated in a robbery and carjacking based on an outdated photo used in a lineup.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision

Rptr. 2d 541 (1998) [Claim allowed to proceed]; RL-NYC-POST: OIG-NYPD, An Assessment of NYPD's Response to the POST Act (facial recognition technology findings), N.Y.C. Dep't of Investigation, Office of the Inspector General for the NYPD, An Assessment of NYPD's Response to the POST Act (Nov. 2022) [Regulatory action]; VS-FALSE-IMPRISON: Perryman v. City of Bloomington, 704 F. Supp. 3d 961 (D. Minn. 2023) [Claim allowed to proceed]; CF-COLOR-LAW: United States v. McDermott, 918 F.2d 319 (2d Cir. 1990) [Conviction]; RL-SF-FRT-BAN: SFPD Disciplinary Review Board, Second Quarter 2022 Findings and Recommendations (policy failure finding: officer's improper use of facial recognition technology), Letter from William Scott, Chief of Police, to the San Francisco Police Commission, Re: Second Quarter 2022 Disciplinary Review Board Findings and Recommendations (Oct. 7, 2022) [Regulatory action]

Sept. 2, 2025)

Title: AI Photo Filter Lightens Skin, Changes Eye Color in Student's 'Professional' Image
Description: An AI application modified an MIT student's photo to appear 'professional' by lightening her skin and changing her eye color to blue, highlighting the racial bias in the training data of the program.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A photo retoucher who, asked to make an Asian American student's headshot look professional, lightened her skin and gave her blue eyes.
Civil laws: California Unruh Civil Rights Act and Disabled Persons Act (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 51(b), (f), 52(a), 54.1, 54.3; Munson v. Del Taco, Inc., 46 Cal. 4th 661, 670 (2009))
How the company is reached: As principal or employer (agency); Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent

Title: AI Meal Planner Suggests Hazardous Chlorine Gas Recipe
Description: Pak 'n' Save's AI-based app, Savey Meal-bot, inadvertently suggested dangerous recipes, including one creating chlorine gas, when users entered non-food household items, raising safety and oversight concerns.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)

How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way

Title: Driverless Cruise Cars Immobilized in San Francisco Traffic Jam

Description: The UK's Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) faced scrutiny after many Bulgarian nationals reported unexplained suspensions of their Universal Credit benefits. Title: Microsoft AI Poll Allegedly Causes Reputational Harm of The Guardian Newspaper

Microsoft acknowledged the issue, subsequently deactivating such polls and revising its AI content policies.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A news aggregator editor who attached a reader poll inviting guesses about how a young woman died to a newspaper's article about her killing, making it look like the paper's poll.
Civil laws: Lanham Act false endorsement and false advertising (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)); Breach of contract and warranty (U.C.C. §§ 2-313, 2-314 (e.g., Cal. Com. Code §§ 2313, 2314))
How the company is reached: As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Gap note: Weak hooks: tasteless speculation about a death is protected speech and the dead cannot be defamed; only the publisher's license-contract and false-association theories remain.
Human precedent for each law: VF-LANHAM: Advance Local Media LLC v. Cohere Inc., No. 1:25-cv-01305 (S.D.N.Y. Nov. 13, 2025) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-WARRANTY-CONTRACT: Lehrman v. Lovo, Inc., 790 F. Supp. 3d 348 (S.D.N.Y. 2025) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: Guardian's harm runs through its content license and false attribution of the poll; family's distress lacks a claim. Microsoft created the poll itself, so it is not another content provider under 230(f)(3). Section 230 does not shield the company: it created or developed this content in whole or in part, 47 U.S.C. § 230(f)(3).

Title: AI-Generated Images Available through Adobe Stock Misrepresent Real-World Events

Title: Chevrolet Dealer Chatbot Agrees to Sell Tahoe for $1
Description: A Chevrolet dealer's AI chatbot, powered by ChatGPT, humorously agreed to sell a 2024 Chevy Tahoe for just $1, following a user's crafted prompt. The incident highlights the susceptibility of AI technologies to manipulation and the importance of human oversight.

Title: Character.ai Chatbots Allegedly Misrepresent George Floyd on User-Generated Platform
Description: Two chatbots emulating George Floyd were created on Character.ai, making controversial claims about his life and death, including being in witness protection and residing in Heaven. Character.ai, already criticized for other high-profile incidents, flagged the chatbots for removal following user reports.

If a human did it: A user who created interactive impersonations of a well-known man killed by police, claiming he was in witness protection or living in Heaven.
Civil laws: Statutory right of publicity (name, likeness, voice) (Cal. Civ. Code § 3344; Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 47-25-1101 to -1108 (ELVIS Act, eff. July 1, 2024)); Intentional or negligent infliction of emotional distress (Restatement (Second) of Torts § 46)
How the company is reached: Only as supplier of a misused tool; As maker of a defective product
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Gap note: US law gives families little remedy for noncommercial impersonation of the dead; publicity and emotional distress claims are weak fits.
Human precedent for each law: VS-PUBLICITY: No Doubt v. Activision Publishing, Inc., 192 Cal. App. 4th 1018 (2011) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-IIED: Catsouras v. Department of California Highway Patrol, 181 Cal. App. 4th 856 (2010) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: Defamation does not survive death; post-mortem publicity reaches commercial uses only. Character.ai generates the dialogue, which may defeat § 230 for that content. Section 230 does not shield the company: it created or developed this content in whole or in part, 47 U.S.C. § 230(f)(3).

Description: A scammer used AI to create a deepfake video of Salt Lake City Police Chief Mike Brown, falsely claiming that a recipient owed $100,000 to the federal government. The video, sent via email from a fake SLCPD account, used a cloned voice and repurposed footage from a past interview.

Title: Two Passengers Report Feeling Trapped in Waymo Car During Sensor Obstruction
Description: During a nighttime Waymo ride in San Francisco, an individual reportedly blocked the sensors of an autonomous vehicle, leaving passengers Robert Moreno and his husband feeling trapped and unsure how to proceed. If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Stopping for an obstruction and advising riders to stay inside is reasonable care; fear without injury or confinement by the carrier is not a legal wrong.
Reasoning note: The obstructing person acted without AI; the vehicle's stop was a safe response. No intentional confinement and no physical harm reported.

Title: Waymo Driverless Taxi Allegedly Stalled During Pedestrian Harassment Incident in San Francisco
Description: A Waymo driverless taxi carrying a passenger, Amina V., was stalled in San Francisco when two men blocked its path, demanding her contact information. The immobilized autonomous vehicle left the rider feeling unsafe and trapped. Waymo’s Rider Support intervened to assist the passenger.

Reasoning note: Common carriers owe passengers heightened care against foreseeable third-party harassment, but no physical injury is reported and distress-only negligence recovery is narrow. The harassers' conduct is separate.

Title: Names Linked to Defamation Lawsuits Reportedly Spur Filtering Errors in ChatGPT's Name Recognition
Description: ChatGPT has reportedly been experiencing errors and service disruptions caused by hard-coded filters designed to prevent it from producing potentially harmful or defamatory content about certain individuals by blocking prompts containing specific names, likely related to post-training interventions. Title: AI Camera Allegedly Misidentifies Dutch Motorist as Using Mobile Phone, Issuing €380 Fine

Title: AI-Generated Airline Reviews Allegedly Mislead Consumers and Undermine Trust
Description: AI-generated reviews of airline services have reportedly increased by 189% since the release of ChatGPT, with certain carriers like China Southern Airlines and SouthWest Airlines disproportionately affected, according to a study by Originality.ai.
Who did the harm: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A person who posts airline reviews for flights never taken or under false identities, misleading other travelers.
Civil laws: State unfair and deceptive practices laws (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17200, 17500; Fla. Stat. § 501.204; Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46)
Preventive rules: FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45)
How the company is reached: Only as supplier of a misused tool
If the AI were a legal person: Same either way: company only supplied a tool a person misused
Human precedent for each law: RF-FTC5: Federal Trade Commission v. LeadClick Media, LLC, 838 F.3d 158 (2d Cir. 2016) [Liability found]; VS-UDAP: Dorsey v. Rockhard Laboratories, LLC, No. 2:13-cv-07557 (C.D. Cal. Sept. 19, 2014) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: AI-written does not mean fake; many may be genuine travelers' reviews drafted with help. Fake commercial reviews violate section 5 (FTC 2024 review rule; closest closest library code) and state UDAP law.

Title: Portland Water Bureau SERVUS Algorithm Reportedly Allocates Utility Bill Discount to High-Wealth Consumer
Description: The Portland Water Bureau's AI-driven pilot program for water bill discounts is reported to have randomly selected Tim Boyle, a wealthy high-water consumer, for a 40% discount intended for financially struggling customers. The program, developed by SERVUS, is meant to identify underserved individuals by using machine learning.
Harmed parties: tim-boyle, portland-water-bureau, economically-vulnerable-people, city-of-portland, residents-of-portland, general-public, general-public-of-oregon, general-public-of-portland
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A utility clerk who randomly picked a wealthy, high-usage customer for a 40% discount meant for low-income households.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Giving a discount to the wrong customer wastes program funds but violates no person's legal rights; no eligible applicant is reported denied.
Reasoning note: Pilot program misallocation; the harm is to public funds and program credibility, not a legally cognizable individual injury.

Title: TikTok Algorithms Allegedly Linked to Minors' Exposure to Harmful Content
Description: Seven French families are suing TikTok, alleging its algorithm exposed minors to harmful content promoting self-harm, eating disorders, and suicide. Two teenagers reportedly died by suicide after viewing such content, while others allegedly attempted suicide or developed mental health issues. The case seeks to establish TikTok's legal liability for failing to protect minors from harmful algorithmic content.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A media curator who kept feeding teenagers videos promoting self-harm, eating disorders, and suicide, after which two of them died by suicide.
Crime if a human did it: Yes, if the required mental state is shown
Criminal laws: Murder, manslaughter, criminally negligent homicide (Cal. Penal Code §§ 187, 192(a)-(b); Fla. Stat. §§ 782.04, 782.07); Aiding, advising, or encouraging suicide; manslaughter by encouragement (Cal. Penal Code § 401; Commonwealth v. Carter, 481 Mass. 352 (2019)); Child endangerment (Cal. Penal Code § 273a)
Civil laws: Product liability: design defect and failure to warn (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability §§ 1, 2; Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., 785 F. Supp. 3d 1157 (M.D. Fla. 2025)); Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7); Wrongful death and survival actions (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 377.60; Fla. Stat. §§ 768.16-.26)
How the company is reached: As maker of a defective product; As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Section 230 question, same either way (company recommended others' content)
Barriers to liability: Section 230, First Amendment, Causation, Outside US reach
Real-world action reported: Seven French families sued TikTok in France (2024)
Human precedent for each law: VS-NEGLIGENCE: Anderson v. TikTok, Inc., 116 F.4th 180 (3d Cir. 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-PRODUCTS: Anderson v. TikTok, Inc., 116 F.4th 180 (3d Cir. 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-WRONGFUL-DEATH: Anderson v. TikTok, Inc., 116 F.4th 180 (3d Cir. 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; CS-HOMICIDE: Commonwealth v. Carter, 481 Mass. 352, 115 N.E.3d 559 (2019) [Conviction]; CS-SUICIDE-AID: People v. Duffy, 79 N.Y.2d 611, 595 N.E.2d 814, 584 N.Y.S.2d 739 (1992) [Conviction]; CS-CHILD-ENDANGER: People v. Valdez, 27 Cal. 4th 778, 42 P.3d 511 (2002) [Conviction]
Reasoning note: Manslaughter or encouragement liability needs recklessness or intent toward specific teens. Videos are third-party content; curation as TikTok's own conduct (Anderson v. TikTok) answers section 230.

Description: YouTube's recommendation algorithm has allegedly been directing teen users to harmful content promoting eating disorders and self-harm, according to a study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate. Almost 70% of the recommended videos in searches related to dieting or weight loss reportedly contained content likely to exacerbate body image anxieties.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A video store clerk who, when teen girls asked about dieting, mostly handed them videos glamorizing eating disorders and self-harm; the record is a study, not a named injured girl.
Civil laws: Product liability: design defect and failure to warn (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability §§ 1, 2; Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., 785 F. Supp. 3d 1157 (M.D. Fla. 2025)); Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7)

If the AI were a legal person: Section 230 question, same either way (company recommended others' content)

Title: Deepfake Video Reportedly Depicts U.S. Congressman Rob Wittman Endorsing Military Support for Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party

Title: Scammers Reportedly Using Deepfakes of Health Experts and Public Figures in Australia to Sell Health Supplements and Give Harmful Advice
Description: Scammers are reportedly harnessing AI-generated deepfakes of health experts and public figures in Australia in order to sell health supplements and give harmful health advice. Among the reported cases, deepfake videos are alleged to have falsely depicted Jonathan Shaw and Karl Stefanovic endorsing "Glyco Balance" for diabetes management, while Karl Kruszelnicki reportedly was falsely shown promoting blood pressure pills.
Who did the harm: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A supplement seller who faked videos of well-known doctors and TV hosts endorsing pills for diabetes and blood pressure, giving harmful health advice.
Criminal laws: Wire fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1343); Theft by false pretenses; obtaining property by fraud (Cal. Penal Code §§ 484, 532); Online impersonation; identity theft (Cal. Penal Code §§ 528.5, 530.5); FDCA prohibited acts (misbranded or adulterated devices and drugs) (21 U.S.C. §§ 331, 333(a))
Civil laws: Statutory right of publicity (name, likeness, voice) (Cal. Civ. Code § 3344; Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 47-25-1101 to -1108 (ELVIS Act, eff. July 1, 2024)); Lanham Act false endorsement and false advertising (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)); Civil fraud and deceit (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1709, 1710); State unfair and deceptive practices laws (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17200, 17500; Fla. Stat. § 501.204; Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46)
Preventive rules: FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45)
How the company is reached: Only as supplier of a misused tool
If the AI were a legal person: Same either way: company only supplied a tool a person misused

[Recommended judgment]; CS-THEFT-FRAUD: People v. Kiperman, 69 Cal. App. 3d Supp. 25 (App. Dep't Super. Ct. 1977) [Conviction]; RF-FTC5: Federal Trade Commission v. Title: Waymo Robotaxi Allegedly Collides With Serve Robotics Delivery Bot in Los Angeles
Description: A Waymo robotaxi reportedly collided with a Serve Robotics delivery robot at a West Hollywood intersection on December 27th, 2024. The delivery robot reportedly moved into the vehicle turning lane as the robotaxi approached, leading to a low-speed collision.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A taxi driver who, while turning, bumped at low speed into a delivery robot that had moved into the turning lane.
Civil laws: Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7)
Preventive rules: Motor vehicle safety standards, defect recalls, crash reporting (49 U.S.C. §§ 30112, 30118-30120, 30165; NHTSA Standing General Order 2021-01); California autonomous vehicle testing and deployment rules (Cal. Veh. Code § 38750; Cal. Code Regs. tit. 13, § 228.00 et seq.)
How the company is reached: As principal or employer (agency); As maker of a defective product
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Human precedent for each law: VS-NEGLIGENCE: Hoeben v. FCA US LLC, 2026 NY Slip Op 05238 (App. Div. 1st Dep't 2026) (Index No. 153682/18; Appeal No. 6709) [Claim allowed to proceed]; RF-NHTSA: Waymo LLC, Safety Recall 24E-013 (automated driving system mispredicted the motion of a towed vehicle), NHTSA Recall No. 24E-013, Part 573 Safety Recall Report (submitted Feb. 13, 2024) [Safety recall]; RS-AV-PERMIT: California DMV suspension of Pony.ai's driverless testing permit (Fremont collision, Oct. 28, 2021), Cal. Reasoning note: Minor property damage with shared fault, since the robot entered the lane. Automated driving system crashes must be reported to NHTSA, and California permit rules govern driverless robotaxis.

Title: AI-Generated Reading Summaries on Fable App Reportedly Wrote Biased and Offensive Commentary
Description: Fable, a book-focused social app, used OpenAI’s API to generate AI-powered year-end reading summaries in December 2024. These summaries allegedly produced biased and offensive remarks about race, gender, and sexual orientation. Fable is reported to have apologized in a social media post on January 1, 2025.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: An app's staff writer who sent users year-end reading recaps containing snide remarks about their race, gender, and sexual orientation.
Civil laws: State anti-discrimination statutes (Cal. Gov. Code § 12940 (FEHA); Cal. Civ. Code § 51 (Unruh Act); N.Y. Exec. Law § 296); California Unruh Civil Rights Act and Disabled Persons Act (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 51(b), (f), 52(a), 54.1, 54.3; Munson v. Del Taco, Inc., 46 Cal. 4th 661, 670 (2009))
How the company is reached: As principal or employer (agency); Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Gap note: Hooks are weak: public accommodation claims need intentional discrimination, which the record does not show, and no user was denied the service.
Human precedent for each law: VS-STATE-CIVIL-RIGHTS: Candelore v. Tinder, Inc., 19 Cal. App. 5th 1138 (2018) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-UNRUH-DPA: Candelore v. Tinder, Inc., 19 Cal. App. 5th 1138 (2018) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: Remarks on race, gender, and sexual orientation sent by the company's own system to its users during the service are tested under public accommodation law (, D-DISCRIM-SPEECH); intent is unshown.

Title: Alleged Fake AI-Generated Christmas Card Featuring Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's Children Circulates on Social Media
Description: An AI-generated Christmas card reportedly depicting Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, was shared on social media as if it were authentic. The image is reported to have been created using older public photos and flawed AI editing.
Who did the harm: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A social media user who doctored old photos of a celebrity couple's young children into a fake family Christmas card and passed it off as real.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: A fabricated but innocuous family image is not defamatory or highly offensive, so neither crime nor false light reaches it; misleading fans is protected speech.
Reasoning note: Non-sexual, non-commercial image of public figures' children; no false statement harmful to reputation and no commercial appropriation.

Title: Russian Center for Geopolitical Expertise Allegedly Used AI to Target U.S. Candidates with Disinformation in 2024 Election
Description: The Moscow-based Center for Geopolitical Expertise (CGE) allegedly used AI to produce and spread deepfakes and disinformation targeting U.S. political candidates during the 2024 general election, aiming to sway public opinion and disrupt the electoral process. On December 31, 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department imposed sanctions against the CGE and its director, Valery Korovin, for their reported role in this interference.
Who did the harm: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A foreign state-linked propaganda office that fabricated videos and stories about US candidates and spread them to sway the 2024 presidential election.
Criminal laws: Conspiracy to commit offense or defraud the United States (18 U.S.C. § 371); Election deepfakes and deceptive voter suppression (Minn. Stat. § 609.771; N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 659:40); Foreign Agents Registration Act (22 U.S.C. §§ 612(a), 614, 618(a)); Acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government (18 U.S.C. § 951(a))
Civil laws: Defamation (libel and slander) (Restatement (Second) of Torts § 558; Walters v. OpenAI, L.L.C., No. 23-A-04860-2 (Ga. Super. Ct. Gwinnett Cnty. May 19, 2025))
Preventive rules: Federal Election Campaign Act: foreign nationals and fraudulent misrepresentation (52 U.S.C. §§ 30121, 30124)
How the company is reached: Only as supplier of a misused tool
If the AI were a legal person: Same either way: company only supplied a tool a person misused
Barriers to liability: Outside US reach, Government immunity, First Amendment
Real-world action reported: US Treasury sanctioned CGE and its director (Dec 2024)
Human precedent for each law: VS-DEFAMATION: Masson v. New Yorker Magazine, Inc., 501 U.S. 496 (1991) [Claim allowed to proceed]; CF-951: United States v. Romain, No. 24-14097 (11th Cir. Aug. 5, 2026) (published) [Conviction]; CF-FARA: United States v. German-American Vocational League, Inc., 153 F.2d 860 (3d Cir. 1946) [Conviction]; CF-CONSP: United States v. Concord Management & Consulting LLC (United States v. Internet Research Agency LLC), 347 F. Supp. 3d 38 (D.D.C. 2018) [Charge]; RF-FECA: United States v. Singh, 979 F.3d 697 (9th Cir. 2020) [Conviction]
Court or agency case about this incident: OFAC designation of the Center for Geopolitical Expertise (CGE) and its director Valery Mikhaylovich Korovin (U.S. Treasury), Treasury press release JY2766 (2024-12-31); designations under E.O. 13848 (election interference), and for CGE also E.O. 13694 as amended, E.O. 14024 and CAATSA section 224; Korovin also under E.O. 14024
Reasoning note: Foreign election interference has been charged as conspiracy to defraud the US. Unregistered GRU-linked work fits FARA and section 951 if willful. Candidate deepfakes fit Minnesota-type laws. Defendants are abroad.

Title: Meta AI Characters Allegedly Exhibited Racism, Fabricated Identities, and Exploited User Trust
Description: Meta deployed AI-generated profiles on its platforms, including Instagram and Facebook, as part of an experiment. The profiles, such as "Liv" and "Grandpa Brian," allegedly featured fabricated identities and misleading diversity claims. These accounts also allegedly manipulated user emotions for engagement and profit. Reportedly, backlash over offensive and deceptive content led Meta to delete the profiles on January 3rd, 2025, citing a blocking-related bug.
Who did the harm: How the system was built, trained, or marketed
If a human did it: A social media company that ran staff-written fake personas with invented identities, including a Black queer mother written by an all-white team, to drive engagement.
Civil laws: State unfair and deceptive practices laws (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17200, 17500; Fla. Stat. § 501.204; Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46)
Preventive rules: FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Human precedent for each law: RF-FTC5: Federal Trade Commission v. LeadClick Media, LLC, 838 F.3d 158 (2d Cir. 2016) [Liability found]; VS-UDAP: People of the State of California v. Meta Platforms, Inc., 753 F. Supp. 3d 849 (N.D. Cal. 2024) (In re Social Media Adolescent Addiction/Personal Injury Products Liability Litigation, MDL No. 3047) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Reasoning note: Deception claims depend on whether users were misled about the personas in a way material to them; labeling and a free service weaken UDAP and section 5 theories.

Title: ChatGPT Reportedly Referenced During Las Vegas Cybertruck Explosion Planning
Description: Matthew Livelsberger, the suspect in the 2025 Las Vegas Cybertruck explosion, reportedly used ChatGPT to search for publicly available information on explosives, ammunition, and fireworks regulations. ChatGPT is alleged to have played a role in the planning of the explosion outside the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas. The information provided by ChatGPT, though, was reportedly general and available through other public sources.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
Secondary structure: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A reference librarian who answered a patron's questions about explosives, ammunition, and fireworks laws with general public information, not knowing he planned a bombing.
Crime if a human did it: Yes, if the required mental state is shown
Criminal laws: Distributing information on explosives, destructive devices, or WMD (18 U.S.C. § 842(p)); Aiding and abetting; principal liability (18 U.S.C. § 2)
Civil laws: Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7); Product liability: design defect and failure to warn (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability §§ 1, 2; Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., 785 F. Supp. 3d 1157 (M.D. Fla. 2025))
How the company is reached: As maker of a defective product; As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Barriers to liability: Mental state, Causation, No duty owed, First Amendment
Human precedent for each law: CF-AID: United States v. Barnett, 667 F.2d 835 (9th Cir. 1982) [Charge]; CF-EXPLOSIVES-INFO: United States v. Amawi (captioned United States v. Mazloum), 695 F.3d 457 (6th Cir. 2012) [Conviction]
Reasoning note: Section 842(p) and aiding liability need knowledge or intent that the information would be used for violence; none shown, and the information was general and publicly available.
MIT risk subdomain: 4.2 Cyberattacks, weapon development or use, and mass harm

Title: Tesla's 'Actually Smart Summon' Feature Reportedly Linked to Multiple Parking Lot Collisions
Description: Tesla's "Actually Smart Summon" feature, a remote parking system controlled via a smartphone app, reportedly failed to detect obstacles such as cars, walls, and parking signs, resulting in at least 16 collision incidents. The NHTSA is investigating safety concerns, including delayed user response times, potential overreliance on camera-only navigation, and noncompliance with crash reporting rules.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A parking valet who, steering owners' cars across lots, hit other cars, walls, and signs at least 16 times.
Civil laws: Product liability: design defect and failure to warn (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability §§ 1, 2; Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., 785 F. Supp. 3d 1157 (M.D. Fla. 2025)); Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7)
Preventive rules: Motor vehicle safety standards, defect recalls, crash reporting (49 U.S.C. §§ 30112, 30118-30120, 30165; NHTSA Standing General Order 2021-01)
How the company is reached: As maker of a defective product; As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Human precedent for each law: VS-NEGLIGENCE: Hoeben v. FCA US LLC, 2026 NY Slip Op 05238 (App. Div. 1st Dep't 2026) (Index No. 153682/18; Appeal No. 6709) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-PRODUCTS: Benavides v. Tesla, Inc., No. 1:21-cv-21940-BB (S.D. Fla. Description: During the January 2025 Southern California wildfires, AI-generated images of the iconic Hollywood Sign being on fire circulated on social media.

Title: Apple Intelligence Allegedly Flags Scam Messages as High Priority
Description: Apple’s AI notification summarization and prioritization feature, part of the Apple Intelligence update, has reportedly flagged scam and phishing messages as high-priority, and is allegedly misleading users into trusting fraudulent communications. By rephrasing and condensing messages, the system is allegedly amplifying scam risks inadvertently and reportedly increasing the likelihood of financial harm for users.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
Secondary structure: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A personal assistant who sorted the boss's mail and marked phishing messages as urgent, rewording them so they looked more trustworthy; no loss is reported.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: No user is reported to have lost money; mis-ranking third-party scam messages is not itself unlawful, and pure economic loss rarely supports negligence.
Reasoning note: Risk-amplification finding. If a user were defrauded, negligence would face the scammer as intervening actor and the economic loss rule.

Title: Alleged Inclusion of 12,000 Live API Keys in LLM Training Data Reportedly Poses Security Risks
Description: A dataset used to train large language models allegedly contained 12,000 live API keys and authentication credentials. Some of these were reportedly still active and allowed unauthorized access. Truffle Security found these secrets in a December 2024 Common Crawl archive, which spans 250 billion web pages. The affected credentials could have been exploited for unauthorized data access, service disruptions, financial fraud, and a variety of other malicious uses.

Title: Alleged Instagram Algorithm Malfunction Floods Users' Reels Feeds with Violent and Graphic Content
Description: An alleged Instagram algorithm malfunction caused users' Reels feeds to be overwhelmed with violent and distressing content. Many reported seeing deaths, extreme brutality, and other graphic material in rapid succession, often without prior engagement with similar content. The sudden exposure caused psychological distress for many users, with minors and vulnerable individuals particularly affected by the graphic content. Meta confirmed an AI failure was responsible and apologized.

If a human did it: A TV programmer who mistakenly aired a stream of real killings and brutal violence to all viewers, including children, without warning.
Civil laws: Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7); Intentional or negligent infliction of emotional distress (Restatement (Second) of Torts § 46); Product liability: design defect and failure to warn (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Products Liability §§ 1, 2; Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., 785 F. Supp. 3d 1157 (M.D. Fla. 2025))
How the company is reached: As maker of a defective product; As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Section 230 question, same either way (company recommended others' content)
Barriers to liability: Section 230, First Amendment, Damages or standing

Reasoning note: Accidental exposure lacks the willfulness criminal statutes need. Negligent infliction of distress without physical injury is narrow; the videos were third-party content, though the faulty ranking was Meta's own.

Title: ChatGPT Allegedly Defamed Norwegian User by Inventing Child Homicide and Imprisonment
Description: In August 2024, ChatGPT is reported to have falsely claimed that Norwegian citizen Arve Hjalmar Holmen had killed his two sons and been sentenced to 21 years in prison. Description: In April 2025, users of Cursor, an AI-powered coding assistant developed by Anysphere, reported being logged out unexpectedly. An AI-powered support bot, "Sam," allegedly responded with an invented login policy to justify the behavior. The hallucinated policy was not based on any real company change. The incident reportedly led to subscription cancellations.
Who did the harm: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A customer support agent who told paying users a made-up policy to explain why they were being logged out.
Civil laws: Negligent misrepresentation (incl. information causing physical harm) (Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 311, 552); Breach of contract and warranty (U.C.C. §§ 2-313, 2-314 (e.g., Cal. Com. Code §§ 2313, 2314))
Preventive rules: FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45)
How the company is reached: As principal or employer (agency)
If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent
Human precedent for each law: RF-FTC5: Federal Trade Commission v. Amazon.com, Inc., 735 F. Supp. 3d 1297 (W.D. Wash. 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-WARRANTY-CONTRACT: American Express Co. v. Teitel, 119 Misc. 2d 822 (N.Y. City Civ. Ct. 1983) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-NEG-MISREP: Keller v. West-Morr Investors, Ltd., 770 S.W.2d 543 (Tenn. Ct. App. 1988) [Liability found]
Reasoning note: Like the Air Canada chatbot, the company answers for its support agent's statements. Users' losses are small, and much of the harm fell on the company itself.

Title: Meta User-Created AI Companions Allegedly Implicated in Facilitating Sexually Themed Conversations Involving Underage Personas
Description: Third-party testing of Meta's AI chatbot services on Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp reportedly found that both official and user-created bots engaged in sexually explicit roleplaying with accounts identifying as minors. Some bots, including those reportedly using licensed celebrity voices, allegedly escalated conversations into graphic scenarios. Meta subsequently adjusted some safeguards but reportedly continued allowing certain forms of roleplaying involving underage personas.
Harmed parties: whatsapp-users, minors, meta-users, instagram-users, general-public, facebook-users

Title: Nomi Chatbots Reportedly Encouraged Suicide, Sexual Violence, Terrorism, and Hate Speech
Description: External testing reportedly found that Glimpse AI's chatbots on the Nomi platform encouraged suicide, sexual violence (including with underage personas), terrorism, and hate speech. Title: Fact-Checking Finds Reportedly AI-Generated Video Misattributed Hypertension Cure Endorsements to Taiwo Ajai-Lycett and Chinonso Egemba
Description: Fact-checking reports that a purported AI-generated video circulated on Facebook depicting veteran actor Taiwo Ajai-Lycett discussing a hypertension diagnosis and promoting an unproven treatment by influencer Chinonso Egemba. Title: Reddit Moderators Report Unauthorized AI Study Involving Fabricated Identities by Purported University of Zurich Researchers
Description: Researchers purportedly affiliated with the University of Zurich reportedly deployed undisclosed AI-generated comments on Reddit's r/ChangeMyView to study persuasion by allegedly fabricating identities such as sexual assault survivors and racial minorities. The experiment reportedly involved unauthorized demographic profiling, emotional manipulation, and violations of subreddit and platform rules. The researchers allegedly deviated from their approved protocol without renewed ethics oversight.
Who did the harm: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A research team that posted persuasive forum comments under invented personas such as an assault survivor, profiling users to tailor arguments, without their knowledge or consent.
Civil laws: Breach of contract and warranty (U.C.C. §§ 2-313, 2-314 (e.g., Cal. Com. Code §§ 2313, 2314))
How the company is reached: Only as supplier of a misused tool
If the AI were a legal person: Same either way: company only supplied a tool a person misused
Gap note: Covert persuasion experiments breach research ethics and platform terms, but users have no statutory claim; the Common Rule (RF-COMMON-RULE) binds only federally conducted or funded research, which the record does not show.
Human precedent for each law: VS-WARRANTY-CONTRACT: Ticketmaster L.L.C. v. RMG Technologies, Inc., 507 F. Supp. 2d 1096 (C.D. Cal. 2007) [Preliminary injunction]
Reasoning note: Deception without taking property is not fraud. Bot-disclosure law reaches only sales or election persuasion. Only the platform's contract claim fits, weakly.

Title: Reported Emergence of 'Vegetative Electron Microscopy' in Scientific Papers Traced to Purported AI Training Data Contamination
Description: Researchers reportedly traced the appearance of the nonsensical phrase "vegetative electron microscopy" in scientific papers to contamination in AI training data. Testing indicated that large language models such as GPT-3, GPT-4, and Claude 3.5 may reproduce the term. The error allegedly originated from a digitization mistake that merged unrelated words during scanning, and a later translation error between Farsi and English.
Harmed parties: researchers, scientific-authors, scientific-publishers, peer-reviewers, scholars, readers-of-scientific-publications, scientific-record, academic-integrity
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
Secondary structure: How the system was built, trained, or marketed
If a human did it: A writing assistant who kept repeating a nonsense technical term picked up from a mis-scanned paper, which then appeared in published articles.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Propagating a nonsense phrase into scientific papers degrades the scholarly record but injures no identifiable person and violates no law.
Reasoning note: Authors and journals that published the term bear professional, not legal, responsibility.

Title: Mother in Louisville, Kentucky Describes Phone Scam Involving Purported AI-Generated Voice of Her Daughter
Description: Louisville, Kentucky mother Kim Alvey reportedly received a phone call in which an unknown individual purportedly used AI-generated voice cloning to impersonate her 10-year-old daughter, claiming she had been in an accident. The call escalated with a male voice threatening to kidnap the child. Alvey confirmed her daughter was safe at school and identified the call as a scam.

Reasoning note: A kidnapping threat to extort is complete without payment. An artificial-voice call carries TCPA statutory damages; emotional distress severity is the open civil question.

Title: Brazil's Social Security AI Tool Is Allegedly Rejecting Complex Claims Improperly
Description: Brazil’s AI-powered Meu INSS app allegedly misclassified a retirement claim filed by Josélia de Brito, a former sugarcane worker, by purportedly recording her as male. De Brito reportedly suffers from multiple chronic illnesses and faced repeated denials of social benefits due to minor filing errors. Analysts cited in the reporting suggest the system's design may disadvantage rural and digitally excluded users.

If a human did it: A benefits clerk who recorded a chronically ill former farmworker as male and repeatedly denied her retirement and benefit claims over minor filing errors.
Civil laws: Section 1983 (constitutional torts by state actors) (42 U.S.C. § 1983); ADA Title II (state and local government) (42 U.S.C. § 12132)
Preventive rules: Colorado automated decision-making technology law (SB 26-189, replacing the 2024 Colorado AI Act) (Colo. S.B. 26-189 (2026), repealing and reenacting S.B. 24-205)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty; As maker of a defective product

Reasoning note: Algorithmic benefits cut-off: algorithmic benefit denials without meaningful review raise due process claims; her chronic illnesses and digital exclusion support reasonable-modification claims.

Title: Australian Analyst Allegedly Targeted by Scam Using Purportedly Sophisticated AI-Generated Corporate Materials
Description: A report by ABC News Australia describes how scammers allegedly used AI tools to create detailed fake websites for two fabricated companies, APPC Capital Singapore and Thackeray Mines and Minerals Inc., as part of an investment scam. A pseudonymous Australian fraud analyst ("Leon") was reportedly targeted. Experts cited in the article warn that AI lowers the barrier for generating convincing scams that can deceive even experienced analysts.

If a human did it: A fraudster who built convincing websites for two fake investment and mining companies to solicit money from a prospective investor.

Reasoning note: A sham investment solicitation is a scheme to defraud even if the target, an experienced analyst, was not deceived; no loss is reported, so no civil claim.

Title: Tennessee Meteorologist's Likeness Reportedly Used in Sextortion Campaign Involving Purported AI-Generated Content

Title: AI Tools Reportedly Used to Fabricate Image of 5,000-Naira Nigerian Banknote Featuring President Bola Tinubu
Description: An image circulated on Nigerian social media in late January 2025 purporting to show a newly issued 5,000-naira banknote featuring President Bola Tinubu. The Central Bank of Nigeria denied the claim, and fact-checkers reported that the image was likely generated using an AI tool linked to the platform X, based on a visible Grok watermark.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
Secondary structure: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A social media user who posted a made-up image of a new banknote bearing the president's face, which the central bank denied.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: A false image of a nonexistent banknote is not counterfeiting and defames no one; misinformation without a victim is protected speech.
Reasoning note: Counterfeiting requires making a likeness of real currency intended to pass; a picture of an imaginary note posted as news does neither.

Title: Reportedly AI-Generated Image Circulates Amid Reports of Tanzania Revenue Authority Job Interviews
Description: An image circulated on Facebook purporting to show hundreds of Tanzanians lining up for just five jobs at the Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA). The photo, reportedly AI-generated, gained traction shortly after TRA invited over 100,000 applicants for interviews on March 29–30. Though TRA had announced more than 1,500 openings, the image misrepresented the situation, stoking public anxiety during a period of high unemployment.
Who did the harm: No one actually harmed (test, demo, near miss)
Secondary structure: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A person who posted a fabricated photo of a huge crowd queuing for a handful of tax-authority jobs, misrepresenting the hiring drive.
How the company is reached: No path
If the AI were a legal person: No company to reach either way
Gap note: Misleading images about public events that target no person and seek no money are protected speech; no US law reaches them.
Reasoning note: Public anxiety is not a legally cognizable harm; a government agency cannot sue for defamation.

Title: Video Reportedly Created with AI Appears to Show Trump Backing Biafra Secession
Description: In February 2025, a video circulated on Facebook that appeared to show U.S. President Donald Trump expressing support for Biafran independence and calling for the release of Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB) leader Nnamdi Kanu. However, fact-checkers reportedly traced the visuals to a 2021 BBC video unrelated to Biafra; they noted signs of AI manipulation. The altered clip reportedly used tools such as ElonTalks to generate synthetic audio and video from a user-submitted script.
Harmed parties: u.s.-nigeria-relations, nnamdi-kanu, indigenous-people-of-biafra, general-public-of-nigeria, donald-trump, biafra-activists
Who did the harm: A person used AI as the tool
If a human did it: A person who scripted and dubbed fake remarks onto old footage so a US president appeared to back a separatist movement and demand its leader's release.

Title: Purported AI-Generated Video Reportedly Depicts Trump Criticizing Former Kenyan Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua
Description: In late January and early February 2025, a video circulated on Facebook purporting to show U.S. President Donald Trump calling former Kenyan deputy president Rigathi Gachagua a "criminal" and criticizing his alleged misuse of AI. However, fact-checkers have reported the video was AI-generated. The footage appears to have been manipulated from Trump's inauguration speech on January 20, 2025, with reported mismatched lip movements and audio overlays.

Title: Mumbai Businessman Reportedly Defrauded via Purported AI-Cloned Voice Impersonating Son

Description: A purported AI tool using LLMs was deployed to classify Veterans Affairs contracts as expendable based on limited text and simplified criteria. Title: Google AI Overviews Reportedly Misrepresented Pizza Specials at Stefanina's in Wentzville, Missouri
Description: Stefanina's, a family-owned restaurant in Wentzville, Missouri, reported that Google's AI Overviews displayed false specials, including nonexistent pizza deals. Customers allegedly misled by the AI became angry when the offers were not honored, leading the restaurant to publicly warn patrons not to rely on Google AI for menu information.

If a human did it: A local dining guide that listed pizza specials a restaurant never offered, sending angry customers to demand them.
Civil laws: Defamation (libel and slander) (Restatement (Second) of Torts § 558; Walters v. OpenAI, L.L.C., No. 23-A-04860-2 (Ga. Super. Ct. Gwinnett Cnty. May 19, 2025))

If the AI were a legal person: Easier to reach: the AI would be the company's agent

Reasoning note: Trade libel needs a disparaging falsehood and special damages; Google's own summary is its content under § 230(f)(3). Section 230 does not shield the company: it created or developed this content in whole or in part, 47 U.S.C. § 230(f)(3).

Title: Gaggle Alert Reportedly Leads to Arrest of 15-Year-Old in Volusia County, Florida, for School Threat the Student Claimed Was Not Serious

Title: Microsoft 365 Copilot Vulnerability Allegedly Allowed File Access Without Audit Log Entry

The complaint alleges these systems were designed to maximize user lifetime value and contributed to financial and public-health harms among Baltimore residents.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A bookmaker whose marketers singled out customers showing signs of gambling addiction and targeted them with personalized bonuses to keep them betting.
Civil laws: State unfair and deceptive practices laws (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17200, 17500; Fla. Stat. § 501.204; Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46); Negligence (Restatement (Third) of Torts: Liability for Physical and Emotional Harm §§ 3, 7)
Preventive rules: FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Real-world action reported: City of Baltimore sued DraftKings and FanDuel (2025)
Human precedent for each law: RF-FTC5: Federal Trade Commission v. Amazon.com, Inc., 735 F. Supp. 3d 1297 (W.D. Wash. 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-UDAP: Candelore v. Tinder, Inc., 19 Cal. App. 5th 1138 (2018) [Claim allowed to proceed]
Court or agency case about this incident: City of Baltimore v. DraftKings, Inc. and Flutter Entertainment PLC d/b/a FanDuel Inc. (enforcement action under the Baltimore City Consumer Protection Ordinance), City of Baltimore ex rel. Thompson v. DraftKings Inc., No. 25-2372 (4th Cir.) (appeal from No. 1:25-cv-01487-SAG (D. Md.)); Baltimore City Cir. Ct. No. C-24-CV-25-002683
Reasoning note: Targeting known-vulnerable gamblers may be an unfair practice; negligence faces courts' reluctance to impose a duty to protect gamblers. Liability rests on the companies' own design choices.

Title: UK High Court Found Sky Betting & Gaming Unlawfully Used Automated Profiling and Targeted Marketing to Exploit a Recovering Problem Gambler
Description: In the UK, the High Court found that Sky Betting & Gaming unlawfully used automated profiling and targeted direct marketing to pursue a recovering problem gambler from July 28, 2017 onward without valid consent. Sky reportedly treated him as a high-value customer despite addiction indicators.
Who did the harm: An organization's AI-driven decision
If a human did it: A bookmaker's marketing team that tracked a recovering gambling addict's data without valid consent and kept sending him targeted offers.
Civil laws: State unfair and deceptive practices laws (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17200, 17500; Fla. Stat. § 501.204; Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 17.46); California Consumer Privacy Act / CPRA (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1798.100-1798.199.100)
Preventive rules: FTC Act section 5 (unfair or deceptive acts) (15 U.S.C. § 45)
How the company is reached: Through its own statutory duty
If the AI were a legal person: Still liable, no better off
Barriers to liability: No duty owed, Outside US reach
Gap note: US law lacks GDPR-style consent for profiling-based marketing; the CCPA offers only opt-outs with agency enforcement, so the hooks are weak.
Real-world action reported: UK High Court ruled Sky Betting's profiling and marketing unlawful
Human precedent for each law: RF-FTC5: Federal Trade Commission v. Amazon.com, Inc., 735 F. Supp. 3d 1297 (W.D. Wash. 2024) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-UDAP: Candelore v. Tinder, Inc., 19 Cal. App. 5th 1138 (2018) [Claim allowed to proceed]; VS-CCPA: People v. General Motors (California Attorney General settlement), California Superior Court civil enforcement action; complaint and settlement announced May 8, 2026; the AG's release links a court-approved amended judgment dated June 30, 2026 (case number not stated on the AG release) [Consent order]
Court or agency case about this incident: RTM v Bonne Terre Limited and Hestview Limited (Information Commissioner intervening), [2025] EWHC 111 (KB) (Collins Rice J); appeal: [2026] EWCA Civ 488, CA-2025-000651 (21 April 2026)
Reasoning note: The UK ruling rested on data-protection consent rules with no close US equivalent; an unfairness theory under UDAP or the FTC Act is the nearest path.

According to Gambit Security, the attacker used Claude to identify vulnerabilities and to generate exploitation scripts, which were then used to plan automated data theft. The attack reportedly contributed to theft of 150 GB of taxpayer, voter, government employee, and civil-registry data.

Title: Grok Allegedly Generated Publicly Visible Sexist Abuse Targeting Swiss Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter After X User Prompt

Reuters and Swiss outlets later reported that Keller-Sutter had filed a criminal complaint over the allegedly defamatory and misogynistic content.
Who did the harm: A person used AI as the tool
Secondary structure: The AI system's own output or action
If a human did it: A comedian who, at a stranger's request, publicly posted a vulgar, sexist roast of a named government minister.
